 Favourites stay perfect in Manning Cup second round 







KINGSTON, Jamaica — Top contenders Kingston College (KC), Excelsior High, Mona High, St Andrew Technical High School (STATHS) and Eltham High maintained their perfect starts in the ISSA Manning Cup second round, which was completed on Wednesday.

KC were among the biggest winners, crushing Edith Dalton James High 9-0 to move to six points in Group Three. They had opened their account with a 5-0 win over Penwood High last week. The famed Purples have now rattled in 14 goals from two games, the most in the second round.

St Andrew Technical High School (STATHS) also enjoyed a comfortable outing, defeating Tivoli Gardens High 4-0 to maintain their perfect record to be on six points, but second in Group Three on goal difference. Tivoli remain on three points, level with St George’s College which whipped Penwood High 8-0 for their first win. Penwood and Edith Dalton are at the bottom without a point.

In Group A, the embattled Jamaica College drew 0-0 with Campion College to be at the bottom with one point. St Catherine High lead the group with six points after edging Camperdown High 1-0. Wolmer’s, which hammered Jose Marti 9-1, are second in the group with three points, the same as Camperdown and Jose Marti.

Mona High also continued their impressive form in Group Four, defeating Bridgeport High 5-2 to remain on six points and share the lead with Eltham High which defeated Vauxhall High 4-1. Vauxhall are third on three points, the same as Hillel Academy which edged Denham Town 2-1.

Defending champions Excelsior High also strengthened their position in Group Two with a 2-1 victory over Calabar High. The champions moved to six points from two matches, while Calabar remained on three points.

Charlie Smith High also kept their hopes alive with a 2-1 win over Norman Manley High to be on three points, alongside Calabar. Norman Manley and St Jago are on three points following their 2-1 win over Holy Trinity, who remain pointless.

 Flight attendant among two held in NMIA cocaine seizures 







KINGSTON, Jamaica — Two men, including a flight attendant, have been arrested after police seized more than nine kilogrammes of cocaine in separate incidents at the Norman Manley International Airport (NMIA) on Monday.

A follow-up operation at the flight attendant’s Kingston residence also resulted in the seizure of a firearm and more than 120 rounds of ammunition.

In the first incident, about 8:00 am, the flight attendant was preparing to board a JetBlue Airways flight to New York in the United States when routine security screening revealed anomalies in his luggage.

A detailed search by detectives assigned to the Firearm and Narcotics Investigation Division (FNID) uncovered two rectangular packages containing 3.4 kilogrammes (7.5 pounds) of cocaine, with an estimated street value of $2.9 million. He was subsequently taken into custody.

About 1:30 pm, investigators conducted a follow-up operation at his Kingston residence, where they seized a licensed 9mm pistol and the over 120 rounds of ammunition.

In a separate incident, about 1:32 pm, a man arrived at the airport to board a flight to Canada when security screening revealed anomalies in his luggage.

A subsequent search uncovered 5.6 kilogrammes (12.5 pounds) of cocaine, with an estimated street value of $4.78 million. The man was also arrested.

Both men remain in police custody as investigations continue. Their identities are being withheld pending further investigations.

 Trump says he wants to see Pope ‘get well’ 







BULLHEAD CITY, United States (AFP) — United States (US) President Donald Trump said Wednesday that he wants to see Pope Leo XIV “get well” after the pontiff underwent surgery in Rome this week to remove a cancerous tumor.

“I want to see Pope Leo get well,” Trump told reporters after addressing a campaign rally in Arizona. “It’s big stuff. Anytime you have cancer, but the prognosis seems to be good.”

“I just want to wish him well. Get better fast,” the president added.

Pope Leo’s doctors said Wednesday that he was out of bed, walking and eating after the removal of a cancerous tumor from his lung.

Now the 71-year-old awaits the results of a biopsy to determine if the cancer has spread.

Prayers for the recovery of the Catholic leader of 1.4 billion faithful have been sent from around the world, from the northern Peru city of Chiclayo where he was bishop for eight years, to his US hometown of Chicago and beyond.

Other global leaders also offered best wishes, including Britain’s King Charles III, who is being treated for an undisclosed cancer and last year became his country’s first monarch to pray publicly with the pontiff since the Church of England broke with the Vatican 500 years ago.

Earlier this year, the pope said he has “great love” for the United States, but his stances urging tolerance and protection for migrants, have often put the Vatican at odds with the Trump administration’s crackdown on immigration and use of detention camps.

On Wednesday, Trump also noted that he had spoken to the first American pope’s brother, Louis Prevost, in the past.

“His brother’s a friend of mine who’s a great, he’s a fantastic guy, and his wife. You know, they’re big Trump supporters,” Trump said, adding “his brother loves him a lot, loves the Pope a lot, and that’s good. That’s good enough for me.”

news.title: Ilhan Omar’s Phone Seized, Trump Admin Targeting Her Citizenship: Reports
news.text: Federal authorities investigating Minnesota U.S. Representative Ilhan Omar have seized her phone and issued more than a dozen grand jury subpoenas, including to some of her relatives, according to reports. The moves escalate a probe into her immigration paperwork as President Donald Trump renews attacks on her citizenship just weeks before the midterm elections. The latest developments come two days after federal agents searched the Democrat's Washington, D.C.-area home and a day after Washington, D.C., U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro confirmed a separate investigation into the congresswoman’s financial disclosures, as Newsweek previously reported. The Department of Justice told Newsweek that the October 12 search was part of “an ongoing federal criminal investigation” and confirmed that Homeland Security Investigations agents had executed a judicially authorized search warrant in Washington. Newsweek reached out to Omar’s campaign for comment via email Wednesday night. What We Know About the Ilhan Omar Investigation The subpoenas were issued by a grand jury gathering evidence in Minnesota as federal authorities investigate potential fraud involving Omar’s immigration paperwork, according to a person briefed on the probe who spoke to the Associated Press (AP) on condition of anonymity. The investigation led federal agents to search Omar’s Washington-area residence. The scope of the probe remains unclear, though Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has suggested that authorities are examining potential crimes related to Omar’s family immigration paperwork, according to the AP. Omar has not been publicly charged with a crime in connection with the investigation. On Tuesday, Pirro said that “there are several investigations going on” related to Omar, confirming that her office was also investigating the congresswoman’s financial disclosures. “If there was a crime that was committed, it will be prosecuted,” Pirro said in an interview with Fox News. Authorities have not publicly established if the financial investigation and immigration-related criminal probe are connected. Trump Renews Attacks as Questions About Omar’s Citizenship Resurface The investigations come amid renewed attacks from Trump, who has repeatedly questioned Omar’s background and called for scrutiny of her immigration history. At a rally in Youngstown, Ohio, on Monday, the president criticized Omar’s Somali origins and questioned her right to invoke the U.S. Constitution. “She’s a disaster. She comes in from a country without laws, without police, without military,” Trump said, prompting members of the crowd to chant “deport.” On Tuesday, Trump called Omar a “terrible person” and a “terrible congresswoman.” He also declined to take a position on whether he wanted her deported. Omar arrived in the United States as a refugee and became a naturalized U.S. citizen in 2000. She has represented Minnesota’s 5th Congressional District since 2019 and is seeking reelection in November. The administration’s scrutiny of her immigration history has centered in part on a longstanding allegation that she married her brother to facilitate his entry into the United States. Omar has repeatedly denied the claim, which remains unproven. Constitutional law professor Jonathan Turley said earlier Wednesday that Omar could face denaturalization if the government proves she provided false information that affected her eligibility for citizenship. “The U.S. government’s position has always been that if you have information there that is untrue, where you would not have been made a citizen, then you can be denaturalized,” Turley said during a Fox News interview. He added that the standard of proof in denaturalization cases is high. Omar Calls Search 'Political Intimidation' Ahead of Midterms Omar condemned the search of her home, accusing the Trump administration of using federal law enforcement to target political opponents. “Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement,” Omar wrote on X. “For 10 years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation. I will not be silenced,” she added. The search comes less than three weeks before the November midterm elections, drawing criticism from top Democrats, who called the raid “deeply disturbing.” “For years, Donald Trump and far-right extremists have relentlessly targeted Congresswoman Omar with vile personal attacks and baseless accusations,” an October 12 joint statement from House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and other top congressional Democrats reads. “Now, less than 30 days until the midterm election, his violent mass deportation machine has descended upon the home of a duly elected Member of Congress and her family.” Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Anna Commander and Edward T. Cummins

news.title: Sprawling probes into Ilhan Omar reportedly aim to strip Minnesota lawmaker’s citizenship and deport her
news.text:
By MELISSA KOENIG, US REPORTER 03:53 15 Oct 2026, updated 03:54 15 Oct 2026

Federal investigators are said to be looking for any evidence that could lead authorities to strip Minnesota Congresswoman Ilhan Omar of her American citizenship and deport her.

Omar had been born in Mogadishu, Somalia to an affluent family, who settled in the Washington DC suburbs before they moved to Minnesota as she entered high school. She then gained citizenship through her father in the year 2000.

In order to now strip her of that citizenship, the Justice Department would have to file a lawsuit in federal courts proving she lied in a material way to become a US citizen.

That is reportedly why Homeland Security agents were seen on Monday raiding the progressive lawmaker’s home in Washington DC, just three weeks before the midterm elections in which Omar is seeking re-election.

Agents seized Omar’s cellphone, notebooks, personal computers and her passport in the raid as federal authorities probe Omar’s citizenship status, US officials and people familiar with the investigation told the Wall Street Journal.

Authorities have also issued more than a dozen subpoenas, including to some of Omar’s relatives, seeking testimony before a Minnesota grand jury, the outlet reports.

They are now trying to uncover Omar’s family’s immigration paperwork to determine whether the Democrat or her father, Nur Omar Mohamed, changed her age on her citizenship application to indicate she was 17 years old instead of 18.

If she had been 18 years old when her father became a naturalized citizen, she would have been considered an adult and would have to pursue her own immigration process. But if she was still 17, Omar would have qualified for citizenship automatically when her father’s citizenship was approved.

The Trump administration’s case now hinges on finding material evidence proving that Omar lied about her own age, rather than have her father lie on her behalf, Leon Fresco, a top immigration official in the Justice Department under the Obama administration, told the Journal.

However, when officials at Homeland Security Investigations looked into a similar tip under the Biden administration, federal officials decided not to move forward with the case because they lacked any evidence of fraud.

Omar has repeatedly denied any wrongdoing, saying in September 2018 that she became a citizen ‘before I turned 18’ through her father’s naturalization.

In a statement on Wednesday, staff members at the Democrat’s office also painted the investigation as part of an effort to silence Omar.

‘President Trump would love to eliminate one of the most effective progressive voices in Congress,’ they said in a statement to the Journal, adding ‘there is no basis’ for the investigation.

But it has since been revealed that the congresswoman’s staff pushed to change her birthdate in official state records just months after she first won her seat in 2018.

Omar had been listed as born on October 4, 1981 by the Minnesota Legislative Reference Library throughout her time in the state House. Wikipedia and news outlets including the BBC carried the same date on her biography.

However, in May 2019, her aides asked the library to move the year forward to 1982, according to emails obtained by the New York Post.

The library’s director wrote in one message, sent days after the edit, that Omar’s team had said ‘her birth year was incorrect and requested that we change it to 1982.’

The same email claimed that her aides were lobbying Wikipedia and the Biographical Directory of the United States Congress to make the same birthdate correction.

Federal prosecutors have since served grand jury subpoenas on Omar’s sister, Sahra Noor, and at least one other relative.

Noor runs a Minneapolis-based consulting firm that says it secured ‘more than $20 million in funding for health initiatives and consulted on projects backed by’ the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, United States Agency for International Development and other groups.

As federal investigators now try to find proof that Omar lied on her citizenship application, US Attorney Jeanine Pirro announced that her office will be conducting a probe of the congresswoman’s financial disclosures as well.

‘We’re looking at the facts,’ Pirro told Fox News.

Omar’s 2025 filing had listed assets of between $6 million and $30 million shared with her husband before she amended it to a far smaller range, blaming accounting errors.

The House’s own ethics watchdog had recommended dismissing allegations over the filings last month, a finding Omar’s office has pointed to in her defense.

Still, Omar has long faced allegations, including claims made to the Daily Mail by a Somali community leader, that her 2009 marriage to Ahmed Elmi was intended to help him obtain US immigration status.

Omar denies that Elmi was her brother or that the marriage was fraudulent.

When asked about the search on Monday, Donald Trump told reporters: ‘I have nothing to do with it.’

The president insisted the matter was ‘really up to the DOJ,’ while still branding Omar ‘totally crooked, personally.’

news.title: Mike Tyson and Donald Trump: A Friendship That Raises Questions for Black Men.
news.text:
(ThyBlackMan.com) Here in the stretch before the midterms, the baddest man ever to lace up gloves is right where he always seems to end up, planted somewhere in Donald Trump’s corner. No belt on the line, no pay-per-view audience to impress, nothing to sell but presence itself. Iron Mike is grayer than we remember now, a little softer in the face, yet he carries the same thing he always has, that aura of somebody who simply doesn’t flinch. The 47th president made a campaign stop in Syracuse, New York, on October 9 to support Republican gubernatorial candidate Bruce Blakeman, with the election coming November 3. His old heavyweight friend came along for the ride, lending the cause some muscle. At this point, seeing Tyson standing beside Trump is hardly a surprise anymore.

Which leaves a bunch of us in the fall of 2026 scratching our heads over the same riddle Black men in barbershops from here to Shreveport have turned over for a decade. Why does he keep showing up for a figure like that?

You can’t answer it honestly without rewinding almost 40 years, back when both of them were cash machines wearing different uniforms. Through the late 1980s, while Donald stacked casinos along the Atlantic City boardwalk, the champ was demolishing grown men with a ferocity the boxing world had rarely witnessed. Trump Plaza became closely associated with the fighter’s biggest nights, including the famous 1988 showdown with Michael Spinks at the Atlantic City Convention Hall, right beside the hotel. Trump paid a record $11 million site fee to bring that fight to town. Those were sweaty weekend spectacles where big money, celebrity, and real violence all shared the spotlight. One of them needed packed arenas and headlines. The other wanted paydays and a glittering stage. They fed each other, and the bond was built on something older than ideology, which is plain mutual usefulness.

Then came the fall. Indiana, 1992, when Tyson was convicted of raping Desiree Washington, an 18-year-old beauty pageant contestant, and sentenced to six years in prison. The conviction shattered his career and permanently complicated his public legacy. Here’s where the relationship takes another turn, because the casino boss publicly defended him. Trump questioned the verdict, argued that Tyson had been railroaded, and even suggested allowing him to continue fighting while directing money toward Washington and other rape victims instead of sending him to prison. None of that changes what Tyson was convicted of doing or diminishes the harm Washington suffered. But from the fighter’s perspective, having a powerful friend defend him during the darkest chapter of his public life may have carried enormous weight. Loyalty like that, offered when a man’s reputation has collapsed, can create a sense of obligation that lasts for decades. Looking at their friendship today, I suspect Tyson has never forgotten who spoke up for him.

Jump to 2015, when a reality-TV blowhard rode an escalator into presidential politics, and guess who stepped up early? The champ offered his blessing, praising Trump’s business background and arguing the country ought to run more like a business where the gig goes to whoever can actually do it. Tyson wasn’t blind to every controversy surrounding his friend, either. He acknowledged that some of Trump’s comments about Latinos were crude, even as he defended the man making them. Critics winced. When Trump celebrated the endorsement during the 2016 Republican primary, Ted Cruz condemned him for embracing the support of a man convicted of rape, while Carly Fiorina questioned what that enthusiasm revealed about Trump’s character. None of that seemed to shake Tyson’s support. He had offered a political argument about business and leadership, sure, but I have always suspected something more personal was operating underneath it. He was vouching for somebody who had vouched for him first.

So let me set the real question on the table, the one the headline keeps circling. Is this loyalty, shared values, or honest political agreement?

Strip it down and the policy piece looks thin, at least from where I sit. I’ve listened to this brother talk for 30 years, and not once have I heard him offer some sweeping breakdown of tax brackets, tariffs, or the fine print of Medicaid. Ask about a jab or a left hook and he’ll teach a master class. Raise congressional appropriations and I wouldn’t expect the same enthusiasm. That doesn’t mean Tyson has no political beliefs. His comments about running government like a business tell us he has considered at least some questions of leadership and economic opportunity. But treating his continued support as proof of some deep ideological alignment hands both figures more philosophical credit than the public record earns. There is a difference between believing somebody can lead and embracing every policy that person carries into office.

Values, though, that runs warmer. Each of these characters built an entire life on defiance, on telling polite society precisely where to stick its opinion, on outlasting scandals and setbacks that might have ended somebody else’s public career. Strength, dominance, refusing to surrender, those seem to be the shared scriptures. Two people who have been counted out, laughed at, written off, then found their way back into the spotlight might naturally recognize something familiar in each other. That recognition could explain more than any position paper ever would. Trump sees a former champion who still commands attention when he enters a room. Tyson sees a businessman turned president who has spent decades refusing to retreat when the world turns against him. Neither man has built his public identity around winning everybody’s approval, and that similarity counts for plenty.

Still, I believe loyalty is the engine. Everything else is just trim. When you’ve endured public disgrace and remember that one powerful person defended you while much of the country condemned you, that memory can outlive trophies, outlive presidencies, outlive whatever either of you thinks about the border or the budget. I cannot climb inside Tyson’s head and declare what drives every decision he makes. Nobody outside that friendship can. But watching him stand beside Trump nearly four decades after those Atlantic City nights, I see a man whose allegiance appears rooted in something more enduring than campaign promises. Maybe he agrees with the Republican agenda. Maybe he admires the president’s approach to leadership. My reading is that neither explanation carries quite the same emotional weight as remembering who stood up for him when his own world came crashing down.

I want to sit in the discomfort of it too, because it sits funny with me. That tension is fair, especially for Black men who adore the fighter and can’t stand the ticket he keeps boosting. A person can be grateful to someone who defended him personally and still find himself tangled in a politics that troubles people who once cheered his every victory. Pretending otherwise flattens a whole human being into a cartoon. Plenty of Brothers reading this feel some kind of way watching a Black icon prop up a figure so many of us distrust. Others may share Tyson’s support for Trump and see nothing troubling about the friendship at all. But personal loyalty and public accountability are two different things, and we ought to be grown enough to recognize both. Gratitude doesn’t check your voter registration. It rarely asks whether the friendship helps anybody outside the two people living in it. And defending somebody through a criminal conviction is not the same thing as proving that conviction was unjust.

So what does Tyson’s presence in Syracuse really tell us? From where I stand, he appears to be doing something he has done since those boardwalk days, showing up for a man whose relationship with him has survived extraordinary changes in fortune. His presence beside Trump doesn’t tell us everything about his political philosophy, and it certainly doesn’t require the rest of us to adopt it. What it does reveal is a bond that has endured long after the casinos, championship fights, prison sentence, and presidential campaigns changed both men’s lives. I suspect that personal history matters more to Tyson than most people on either side of the political aisle are willing to acknowledge. You can respect the fidelity while side-eyeing who benefits from it. That blend of admiration and unease might be the most truthful place to land.

Nearly forty years in, the picture speaks for itself, even if the motives behind it remain Tyson’s alone to explain. Whatever you make of the politics, nobody can seriously argue that he has turned his back on Donald Trump. In a culture that ghosts folks the second they stop trending, maybe that stubborn fidelity is the most Tyson thing about him.

Politics explained through the lens of justice and equity. Offering perspective that informs, challenges, and empowers.

news.title: Britain to provide £17m to Chernobyl power plant damaged by Russian drone attack
news.text: Britain has pledged to fund critical repairs to the Chernobyl power plant hit by a Russian drone attack. It comes as Andy Burnham sought to bolster support for Ukraine amid “dark and difficult days” for the war-torn country during Volodymyr Zelensky 's visit to Downing Street. The UK will provide £17 million to help restore its protective shelter and ventilation, which were damaged by an attack last year. Chancellor John Healey said the Government’s commitment to the Ukrainian people was “unshakeable”, while Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said Britain will “stand shoulder to shoulder with Ukraine and will do so until they prevail”. The PM hosted Volodymyr Zelensky in Downing Street on Wednesday, October 14 when he told the Ukrainian president the UK was “behind you and that will not change”. Mr Zelensky received an honour guard made up of troops from the Irish Guards on his arrival at No 10 on Wednesday. The meeting came during a period of strained relations between Ukraine and the US after Donald Trump eased sanctions on Russian diesel last week as high fuel prices in America threatened to overshadow November’s mid-term elections. The UK responded to news of the deal by pledging to “maintain pressure on Russia ”. The US president has also suggested in recent days that Ukraine needs a new leader and claimed Russian leader Vladimir Putin wants a peace deal more than the government in Kyiv. Mr Zelensky has also said use of Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite communications system was “blocked” and that as a result “people will die”, admitting that he felt betrayed by Mr Trump. “It’s a pity that we are losing, we are losing a strong partner,” he told Piers Morgan Uncensored. Starlink is used by Ukraine to defend against aerial attacks and for long-range drones targeting Russian sites. Speaking in the Commons ahead of his meeting with Mr Zelensky, the Prime Minister said he would seek to restore Donald Trump’s support for Ukraine. During Prime Minister’s Questions, Mr Burnham said he was being “careful” in his language after Mr Trump’s diesel deal with Russia, as he said he was “laying the ground” for a reconciliation. He added: “I will listen to President Zelensky carefully, but he won’t be going away from Britain today empty-handed.” During his meeting with Mr Zelensky, he confirmed that the UK would accelerate the supply of crucial air defence missiles to Ukraine amid “heavy bombardment” from Russia. The accelerated support will see faster deliveries of British lightweight multi-role missiles to Ukraine, which have proved effective against Russian jet-powered drones. Russia continues to pound Ukraine’s power grid, as well as oil and gas facilities, after Mr Trump claimed that the two countries had agreed to an “energy ceasefire”. Announcing new funding for repairs at Chernobyl , Mr Healey said: “As the full-scale invasion of Ukraine by Putin continues, our commitment to the Ukrainian people is unshakeable. “We are curtailing the war chest funding Putin so desperately wants and backing the reconstruction of Ukraine that has suffered at the hands of his barbaric attacks.” Mr Miliband said: “Our message to Putin is clear – we stand shoulder to shoulder with Ukraine and will do so until they prevail. “Working with our allies, we are strengthening Ukraine’s security, raising the cost of Russia’s aggression and working towards a just and lasting peace.”
news.summary: Andy Burnham said he 'will listen to President Zelensky carefully' and promised that he would not be leaving Britain 'empty-handed' after his trip to Downing Street
news.author: Peter Hennessy

news.title: James Talarico Defends Unity, Faith, Abortion Rights in Texas Town Hall
news.text: Democratic U.S. Senate candidate James Talarico spent much of a CNN town hall Wednesday night explaining his Christian faith, defending his abortion-rights stance and arguing that Texans have more in common than the political system would have them believe. The former public-school teacher and Presbyterian seminarian student was challenged directly by audience members on abortion, biblical authority, gender-affirming care, national debt, Ukraine and immigration during a series of one-on-one debates that formed the centerpiece of the event. The confrontational format produced some of the clearest examples yet of how Talarico is attempting to build a statewide coalition as he takes on state Attorney General Ken Paxton in the Texas U.S. Senate race. Talarico, seeking to become the first Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate from Texas since 1988, invoked fellow Texan and former President Lyndon B. Johnson as he argued for sending a teacher to Washington. "I am tired of us being divided into teams: left versus right, blue versus red, urban versus rural," Talarico told the audience. "The truth is, we're all on the same team." The message came as the Republican attorney general, who did not attend the event, announced the launch of a statewide bus tour that will start Saturday, according to his post. "Texans don't back down, and neither do I," Paxton wrote on X hours before the event. "I have one message for the far-left extremists who are trying to destroy Texas: Come and Take It." During the town hall, Paxton also attacked Talarico's energy record in a separate social media post, writing that the Democrat had "tried to dismantle the oil and gas industry" and was waging a "war on Texas energy." Newsweek reached out to Paxton's campaign for comment. About 80 minutes into the town hall, Talarico noted that he hadn't mentioned Paxton's name at all. "We cannot afford Ken Paxton's corruption," Talarico said to close the event. Talarico Shares Story on National Stage Talarico, 37, has emerged as one of his party's most recognizable figures in Texas politics. Born in Round Rock, he attended Texas public schools before earning a degree in government from the University of Texas at Austin and a master's degree in education policy from Harvard University. Before entering politics, Talarico taught sixth-grade language arts at Rhodes Middle School in San Antonio, an experience he frequently cites as pivotal in shaping his political worldview. He later worked in educational nonprofit leadership before launching a campaign for the Texas House in 2018, flipping a suburban district previously held by Republicans. A Presbyterian seminarian whose grandfather was a Baptist preacher, Talarico repeatedly emphasized the role faith plays in his public life. "My faith teaches me servant leadership, the idea that being a leader means being a servant," he said. "Over four terms in the Texas House, I've served my constituents, and I'm looking forward to doing that in the U.S. Senate." One of the most striking exchanges came when an independent voter, educator and self-described Orthodox Catholic, challenged Talarico on abortion. She argued that Democrats' support for abortion rights makes it difficult for many Catholics to trust the party on broader questions of human dignity and public policy. Talarico responded by seeking common ground. "You know, some of my spiritual heroes, like Pope Francis and Pope Leo, are pro-life, and they are consistently pro-life," he said. While acknowledging that they reached different conclusions on abortion, Talarico argued that both sides should be able to unite around reducing unwanted pregnancies and abortions. "If we treat this issue as a public health problem and not a culture war problem, then we can actually make progress together," he said. The exchange grew more pointed when Talarico argued that Texas' abortion ban had created dangerous outcomes for women facing medical emergencies. "If we are authentically pro-life, I think we should be disturbed by the outcomes of this extreme abortion ban," he said. Despite their disagreement, the conversation ended cordially, with both participants finding common ground in supporting human life more broadly. Defending His Christian Faith Talarico later faced questions from a Republican voter about past comments concerning gender and theology. Asked directly whether the Bible is "the absolute source of truth and God's final authoritative word," Talarico answered simply: "Yes." The audience member pressed him on previous remarks when he called God nonbinary, a remark that become fodder for Republican campaign attacks. "When I said that, I was being provocative, and I want to admit that and come clean about that," Talarico said. He argued that some of his comments had been misunderstood or stripped of broader theological context. Talarico repeatedly stressed that Christians should be able to disagree without questioning one another's faith. "You are my sister in Christ," he told the voter. "It's OK if you and I have disagreements. That should be encouraged, not discouraged." Talarico Calls National Debt 'Intergenerational Theft' National debt became the focus of another notable exchange when another independent voter challenged Talarico on how he would finance healthcare and education investments while the federal government faces rising debt obligations. Talarico called the debt crisis a moral issue. "We are stealing from future generations," he said. "It is intergenerational theft." He argued the deficit could be reduced by ending what he described as tax loopholes benefiting billionaires and wealthy Americans while pursuing a more restrained foreign policy. He also demanded an end to the war in Iran, which he said is costing taxpayers $1 billion a day. At the same time, he acknowledged that Democrats need to embrace being stewards of taxpayer dollars. "Let me say something that a lot of Democrats aren't willing to say," he said. "We should be looking for efficiency in our government." Ukraine, Iran and Foreign Policy Another voter pressed Talarico on continued U.S. support for Ukraine, questioning why billions are being spent overseas while communities at home continue to face economic hardship. Talarico defended the assistance. "If we can stop [Russian President] Vladimir Putin in Ukraine, then we're not going to have to stop him elsewhere," he said. "In some ways, I see this as a cost-saving measure." He simultaneously criticized American involvement in Iran, arguing the conflict was draining resources, driving up fuel costs and risking additional U.S. casualties. "We should not be sending our brave men and women off to die in another forever war in the Middle East," he said. Talarico on Transgender Issues A later discussion focused on transgender healthcare and government overreach. Talarico said he supports barring gender-transition surgeries for minors while opposing broader restrictions on transgender healthcare. He said he attempted to narrow a Republican-backed Texas bill to focus only on surgical procedures for minors but opposed the final legislation because it extended beyond that. The audience member challenging him argued government should not be involved in those medical decisions at all. The exchange ended with Talarico returning to the economic populism that surfaced repeatedly throughout the night. "Powerful people are using small minorities in our community to distract from their corruption," he said. "The only minority destroying America is the billionaires." ICE and Deportations Talarico also rejected suggestions that he supports abolishing U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), a charge Republicans have frequently leveled against Democrats. Asked about previous comments describing ICE as a "secret police force," Talarico said the agency serves a legitimate purpose but argued recent enforcement actions have crossed a line. "No, and I never have," he said when asked if he supports abolishing ICE. "We need Immigration and Customs Enforcement in this country," he said. Talarico said enforcement should focus on violent criminals, gang members and cartels rather than longtime residents with deep community ties. "We were told that ICE was going to go after violent criminals," he said. "They're going after Uber drivers. They're going after small-business owners. They're going after grandmothers and infants." During the exchange, Talarico cited the case of Lorenzo Salgado, a Houston-area resident who he said had lived in Texas for decades and raised three sons who attended college. "Lorenzo Salgado embodies the American dream," Talarico said. "Lorenzo Salgado was a child of God. Lorenzo, our fellow Texan, deserves justice." Talarico Addresses Social Media 'Spiraling' Talarico started the event by addressing online rumors that emerged after he stepped away from the campaign trail due to illness earlier this month. "I think the responsible thing to do when you have something like the flu is to stay at home and not get other people sick," he said. "That decision to stay home for a week sent my opponent and his conspiracy theorists spiraling." Talarico joked that social media users had falsely claimed he had dropped out of the race, been sent to a mental hospital in Ohio and even died. "Conspiracy theories don't put food on the table. They don't put gas in the tank. They don't actually improve our lives," he said. That message ultimately became the through-line of the town hall. What the Polls Say on Paxton vs. Talarico Talarico has spent the general election courting independents and moderates, while Paxton and the national GOP have tried to tie the Democrat to his party's left wing. Vice President JD Vance rallied for Paxton in East Texas on Tuesday, days after President Donald Trump held a rally in San Antonio. The race remains tight. A Marist poll released Wednesday found Talarico leading Paxton 47 percent to 45 percent among likely voters. Among registered voters, Talarico held a 4-point lead, which was down from 6 points a month earlier. The poll's margin of error for likely voters was plus or minus 4.9 percentage points. The poll offered bright spots for the Democrat among independents, with 52 percent saying they backed Talarico. Paxton's favorability was 22 points underwater, with 34 percent viewing him favorably and 56 percent unfavorably. Despite those numbers, 53 percent of likely voters said they still expect Paxton to win the race. Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Anna Commander and Edward T. Cummins
news.summary: James Talarico tackles immigration, religion and the social media spiral over his campaign absence during a CNN town hall.

news.title: Nobel Peace Prize winner Navi Pillay reflects on career forged under apartheid
news.text:
Even under the thumb of apartheid, Navanethem "Navi" Pillay's school teacher saw potential in the young student, prompting her family to crowdfund for her university application. 

A year after graduating, she became the first woman in her eastern South African province to open a law practice. 

Dr Pillay was the first non-white woman to be appointed to South Africa's High Court, before becoming a judge on the International Criminal Court and later the United Nations' High Commissioner for Human Rights.

In her first Australian interview since receiving the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize last week, Dr Pillay reflected on growing up in a segregated South Africa, her trailblazing career in law, and Trump's "pathetic" criticisms of her.

On growing up under apartheid

Dr Pillay was born on September 23, 1941, in southern Durban, a coastal city in eastern South Africa.

Apartheid was formally codified as government policy seven years later, but Black people had been subject to racial segregation for much longer.

The community Dr Pillay and her six siblings grew up in was designated for people of Indian descent and was constantly under the threat of being declared a white area, which would have meant forced removal.

She said every Christmas her father, who was a bus driver, would drive the family "along the esplanade so we could see the Christmas trees from afar".

"There's no way you could stop and walk along that street," she said.

"You can't go to the beaches, they were all designated for whites only. You couldn't go to the park or use the swings.

Dr Pillay also recalled a time when she was nine or 10 years old and wrote an essay at school about justice. 

"I wrote of two similar cases where the white man got off, but they sentenced the black man to life imprisonment," she said.

"I don't know where I got that [from] … nobody discussed [apartheid] in class.

"We had no newspapers at home. We had no radio, obviously no television.

"So it must have been from the very atmosphere of awareness."

On university and her early days in law

Like her schooling, Dr Pillay was only allowed to attend non-white sections of university. 

She said her law classes were held in a "potato warehouse".

"I was with students who were all involved in some way or another with protest activities and marches on the streets," she said.

"I didn't actually join them, but that's that atmosphere of vibrant awareness of what apartheid is doing to us.

"There was one protest outside our university and the police actually shot at the students."

In 1965, she graduated from the University of Natal with a Bachelor of Laws, before going on to other study, including at Harvard.

Two years after graduating, she opened her own law practice in Natal, becoming the first woman in the province to do so.

On criticisms from Donald Trump

The US president has been vocal about his belief he deserves the Nobel Peace Prize, and was this year nominated by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

He called the Nobel committee's decision this year "disgraceful and embarrassing", saying the prize "has been forever discredited by a handful of radical ideologues who are anti-democracy".

"I don't think I want to be involved in this one-to-one tug of war, but I can't resist commenting that it is such pathetic behaviour to be asking for an award," Dr Pillay said of Trump's criticisms.

"He said things like, 'Some woman got it and nobody knows her.'

On sanctions against the ICC

Just hours after Dr Pillay received the prize, the US announced it would impose sanctions on the International Criminal Court.

Shortly after, Britain, Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, Canada, Japan and the Netherlands issued a joint statement condemning the sanctions, which will freeze the court's assets in the US, as well as block financial transactions and IT agreements the ICC has with US companies.

Australia later added its name to the statement. Dr Pillay said the member states' opposition to the sanctions was "significant".

"We struggle all our lives for states to be seen to be acting collectively. They did so immediately," she said.

"The sanctions are unlawful. They are cruel. It affects everyone."

On Palestine and the Gaza war

From 2021 to 2025, Dr Pillay was the chair of the UN Commission of Inquiry on Occupied Palestinian Territory, which determined last year Israel had committed genocide in the Gaza war.

Israel rejected the report, labelling it "distorted and false".

While the report was the most significant finding by an official body to date, it is not legally binding and does not compel any government to impose sanctions.

Reflecting on what legal weight the finding held, Dr Pillay said the commission remained "the authoritative body on this until a court of law draws its own conclusion and judgment".

"We were given the mandate by member states in the Human Rights Council not only to investigate, find the evidence, but to name the crimes and the individuals," Dr Pillay said.

"What's different about this genocide is it's occurring in real time. So much of the evidence we gathered was seen by the public on television.

"There was a demand and an expectation for answers and for action.

"Every state in the world is obliged to prevent genocide … I reasoned then that because we had a mandate and we could trace, connect these dots, that we can proceed to make findings."

On what she still wants to achieve 

Receiving the world's most prestigious honour at 85 years old, Dr Pillay joked that she could now sleep in every morning. 

Her honest answer, though, was that there was more work to be done.

"I'll stop when human rights violations stop," she said.

"I think I will have to slow down physically, but as long as I can move, I will continue to watch out for the rights of everyone and particularly for justice."

Dr Pillay said her award puts the "focus on justice, international justice [and] the rule of law", which she said were at risk in today's world.
news.summary: In her first Australian interview since winning the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize, Navanethem "Navi" Pillay reflects on growing up in a segregated South Africa, her trailblazing career as a judge, and Trump's "pathetic" criticisms of her.
news.author: Annabel Bowles,Sally Sara

news.title: Donald Trump cancels trip to Bucs-Steelers NFL game this weekend hours after CNN revealed his plans
news.text:
Donald Trump has canceled plans to attend a second football game in as many weeks, according to a report. 

One week after being forced to back out of attending the SEC showdown between Georgia and Alabama, the President has reportedly canceled a trip to an NFL game. 

CNN reported on Tuesday afternoon that Trump was expected to attend the Week 6 clash between the Pittsburgh Steelers and the Tampa Bay Buccaneers at Raymond James Stadium in Florida on Sunday. 

However, the President seemingly pulled a quick U-turn, with the outlet reporting a matter of hours later that he would no longer attend the game. 

The matchup would have marked the second Steelers game that Trump has been in the stands for in two years. 

He also attended the Steelers’ matchup against the New York Jets at Acrisure Stadium in 2024 during his Presidential campaign against Kamala Harris. Pittsburgh proved to be a crucial swing state for the Republican party in the election. 

The U-turn comes less than a week after Trump was also forced to scrap his visit to the college football game between Georgia and Alabama. 

The trip was cancelled due to the arrival of Hurricane Isaias, a Category 3 storm, which made landfall on the Alabama coast on Friday evening.

'Based on the fact that a huge Hurricane/Storm is coming, it is important to have our wonderful First Responders, Law Enforcement, and others, focused on that Storm, and in no way be thinking about the safety, or presence, of the President of the United States, ME!' Trump posted to his Truth Social account on October 9.

'Therefore, I will miss that potentially unbelievable Game, Alabama vs. Georgia but, hopefully, the Game will go on despite the weather! I will be visiting both of those Teams at a later date.'

The southeast of the US has been ravaged by Hurricane Isaias after it hit last Friday night, leaving four people dead and others injured.

The monster storm hit the Florida Panhandle near Destin at around 8.30pm as a Category 2 hurricane, packing maximum sustained winds of 105mph. 

Just 30 minutes later, its winds had fallen to 85mph, but the storm continued to wreak havoc along the Gulf Coast.

The rivalry clash between the Bulldogs and the Crimson Tide still went ahead in Tuscaloosa, Alabama, on Saturday, with the President missing out on a thrilling game. 

Georgia emerged as 20-17 winners at Bryant-Denny Stadium after a controversial finish that saw fans furious at the SEC officials.

With 3:28 left in the game and down by three, Alabama quarterback Keelon Russell fired a second-down pass towards Rico Scott in the end zone.

But Georgia defensive back KJ Bolden didn't play the ball and made contact with Scott without turning his head to the backfield.

Those watching all waited for a flag to be thrown but officials determined it was not pass interference. The next play, Russell was sacked to move them out of field goal range, then Alabama punted and never got the ball back.

Head coach Kaleb DeBoer raged on the sidelines as officials decided not to throw a flag, while ESPN/ABC rules analyst Matt Austin saw a new angle as the Bulldogs kneeled out the clock to end the game.

news.title: Alberta independence vote tests Canada’s unity amid US tensions
news.text:
TORONTO: Alberta voters decide next week if they want the oil-rich province to begin the process of separating from Canada, a pivotal test for the country as it confronts a hostile United States.

Polling indicates less than a quarter of Alberta’s roughly five million people want independence, but in an interview with AFP on Tuesday, a separatist leader insisted those numbers were off.

“I wouldn’t be surprised if we actually win this referendum,” said Mitch Sylvestre, who heads the Alberta Prosperity Project, the most prominent separatist organization.

“I would be very surprised if we got less than 40 percent,” he said.

Monday’s vote is a personal challenge for Prime Minister Mark Carney, who grew up in Alberta and returned there this week to campaign for national unity.

US-Canada hostility triggered by President Donald Trump has defined Carney’s tenure.

Alberta’s oil industry is central to his plans for solidifying Canada’s economy and reducing US reliance.

Carney has backed a new pipeline and other projects to increase crude production, marking a clear break from his predecessor, Justin Trudeau, who was broadly reviled in Alberta over allegations that he stifled oil industry growth in favor of environmental policies.

In a video address on Monday, Canadian Thanksgiving, filmed at his Edmonton high school, Carney highlighted the pipeline as a chance “to create lasting opportunity and prosperity... in this province and across the country.”

“We can’t achieve any of this if we are divided,” he said.

Oil’s prominence in a debate about Canadian unity has highlighted the unusual nature of Alberta’s independence push.

Alberta separatists voice familiar conservative frustrations, from concerns about immigration levels to generalized fears about fraying individual liberty, but their grievances often hinge on oil industry management.

That makes Alberta’s independence movement “mostly an outlier,” said Syracuse University professor Ryan Griffiths, an expert on global separatist groups.

Secessionist movements regularly have “economic motivations,” but typically those are married to a linguistic or nationalist component, Griffiths said.

“There’s no magic line” dictating what defines a nation, he told AFP, but noted Alberta’s case for nationhood appears harder to make than that of other groups, like Catalans, Scots and French-speaking Canadians in Quebec.

Commenting on Alberta’s frustration with Ottawa, Premier Danielle Smith also focused on Trudeau’s alleged hostility to the oil industry.

“When you have a federal government that is actively trying to kill your principal industry, that has a real impact on people,” she told the CBC last week.

Smith says she is voting against independence and has praised Carney’s openness to the oil industry.

She says she called the nonbinding referendum to settle a question dividing the province.

If a majority supports leaving Canada, Smith said she’ll begin the legally binding process of leaving Canada. If a majority votes to stay, she won’t approve another referendum, she told the CBC.

American influence? 

The alleged influence of Trump allies in Alberta has attracted intense scrutiny in Canada.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has called Alberta a “natural partner” for the United States, and Alberta Prosperity Project leaders held several meetings at the State Department.

Earlier this month, Canada’s Globe and Mail newspaper detailed contacts between Sylvestre, his team and Republican Party operatives.

Sylvestre told AFP that, for him, US interests “don’t play any role” in Alberta “until we win and become government,” at which point he would work to ensure free-flowing trade.

“There’s no animosity toward America here,” he said. “I can’t see why we wouldn’t want to continue trading with the biggest economy in the world.”

news.title: Tension erupts during House midterm debate as Lawler fact-checks NY Democrat opponent on immigration
news.text:
Rep. Mike Lawler, R-N.Y., faced off against Democrat opponent Cait Conley Wednesday night in a one-hour debate filled with interruptions and fiery accusations less than three weeks before Election Day.

Lawler is vying for a third term representing New York’s 17th Congressional District, a politically moderate area in the New York City suburbs that could decide the fate of who controls the House of Representatives for the final years of President Donald Trump’s term.

Lawler called out Conley for misrepresenting his voting record, Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act and her own stance on immigration enforcement. Conley, meanwhile, tried to paint Lawler as a Trump acolyte who put the needs of Washington Republicans ahead of the people of his district.

Their most heated clashes came on the immigration front, when the moderator referenced the recent shooting of an illegal immigrant by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents last week in New York City while the man’s 5-year-old child was in the car.

DEM CANDIDATE CLEARS CROWDED FIELD TO FACE TRUMP-BACKED INCUMBENT IN NY

The race between GOP Rep. Mike Lawler and Democrat veteran Cait Conley could decide the fate of the House of Representatives for the next two years. (Eric Lee/Bloomberg via Getty Images; Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

“I believe that border security is national security and that we do need immigration enforcement to ensure that violent criminals and drug cartels and human traffickers and terrorist organizations aren’t in our communities and that they are deported,” Conley said. 

“But what we are seeing right now with the conduct of ICE is posing a public safety hazard. To your point, last week, they shot into a car where there was a 5-year-old child. I’ll tell you, as a law enforcement officer, you’re not permitted to do that kind of stuff.”

NEW YORK GOVERNOR DEBATE HEATS UP AS BLAKEMAN, HOCHUL SPAR OVER TRUMP, SANCTUARY STATUS, ICE SHOOTING

Lawler, however, pointed out the man has a lengthy criminal rap sheet and was seen by some as a danger to his community. He also argued the shooting would never have happened had local law enforcement not been barred from handing him over to ICE by New York’s sanctuary laws.

He said Conley “supports making New York a sanctuary state, prohibits cooperation between local law enforcement and federal immigration officials.”

WATCH: LAWLER UNLOADS ON RASKIN AFTER FIERY IMMIGRATION HEARING: ‘GROW THE F— UP’

Lawler later pivoted the discussion to Sheridan Gorman, the college student from his district who was killed while out with her friends near her campus in Chicago earlier this year. The illegal immigrant accused of killing her was previously charged with shoplifting, but Chicago sanctuary laws prevent local law enforcement from handing him over to ICE.

Police tape cordons off a street in the Marble Hill neighborhood of the Bronx after a shooting involving federal law enforcement agents last week. (WCBS)

Conley called Gorman’s death “an atrocious crime” while repeatedly pointing out it took place in Chicago.

Lawler attempted to intervene multiple times to call it “preventable,” to which an irate Conley responded, “Can I finish?”

“And I do support federal agents and federal law enforcement, federal immigration enforcement, making sure that we deport violent citizens,” she said.

DHS BOSS REVEALS OVAL OFFICE PLAN TO ‘WITHHOLD FUNDING’ FROM SANCTUARY CITIES AFTER AGGRESSIVE NEW YORK BUST

Lawler then argued, however, that Conley’s support of sanctuary policies runs counter to that.

“If you think he should have been deported when he was arrested for shoplifting, he should have been turned over to ICE. Under the new law that you support, he will not be turned over to ICE, and he will be released under cashless bail,” Lawler said.

It prompted the moderator to step in, telling Lawler there was no “cross-examination round.”

Elsewhere in the debate, Lawler accused Conley of having “literally just lied” that Lawler voted with Trump “100% of the time.”

10 DEMOCRAT-HELD HOUSE SEATS REPUBLICANS COULD FLIP TO SAVE THEIR MAJORITY

“I’ve been rated the third most independent member of my conference. And I have taken on the president on numerous issues, including lifting the cap on SALT, including extending Haitian TPS, including passing an extension for the ACA enhanced premium tax credit despite his objections,” Lawler said.

Earlier in the debate, Conley tried to accuse Lawler of supporting tax breaks for companies that build data centers as part of the One Big Beautiful Bill.

Sheridan Gorman and her father, Tom Gorman, in a family photo. (Gorman Family/Fox News)

Lawler shot back, “I know you just moved here from Virginia, so it’s hard for you to understand the local communities, but the fact is … the provision you referenced in the Working Families Tax Cut Act is $80 billion for 100% expensing for every business in America to expense plant, property and equipment. 

“Are you against our small businesses in the Hudson Valley being able to expense their plant, property and equipment and hire more people? Your attack on that rings hollow. You clearly don’t understand what’s actually in the tax bill. And part of the problem is you don’t pay property taxes.”

Both candidates shook hands after their spirited debate and thanked each other for appearing. Lawler also thanked Conley for her military service.

The district is a pivotal one for control of the House next year. Lawler is one of three House Republicans who won a district that former Vice President Kamala Harris also won in 2024. 

And in an election that’s expected to be brutal for the GOP, both sides are pouring millions of dollars into the fight.

news.title: US raises Social Security benefits by 3.6 pc
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Oct 15 (IANS) The United States has announced a 3.6 per cent increase in Social Security benefits for 2027, providing an average additional $75 a month to retired workers as millions of Americans struggle with rising living costs. The Social Security Administration (SSA) said on Wednesday (local time) that nearly 72 million beneficiaries will receive higher payments beginning in January, while approximately 7.3 million people receiving Supplemental Security Income (SSI) will see their increases reflected in payments beginning December 31. The annual cost-of-living adjustment, commonly known as COLA, is designed to help protect the purchasing power of retirees, people with disabilities and other eligible beneficiaries against inflation. The adjustment will affect approximately 76 million Americans across the two programmes, with some individuals receiving benefits under both. "Social Security will implement this cost-of-living adjustment for 76 million Americans, giving them greater financial stability," Social Security Commissioner Frank J. Bisignano said. "Under President Donald J. Trump, Social Security is delivering better, faster, higher-quality service for the American people," he added. According to official figures, the estimated average monthly retirement benefit will rise from $2,095 to $2,170 in January 2027. For retired couples where both spouses receive benefits, the average combined monthly payment is expected to increase from $3,238 to $3,355. The average monthly benefit for workers receiving Social Security Disability Insurance will increase from $1,642 to $1,701. The adjustment also raises federal SSI payment standards, with the maximum monthly payment for an eligible individual increasing from $994 to $1,029. For an eligible couple, the corresponding amount will rise from $1,491 to $1,544. The administration said beneficiaries with personal online Social Security accounts will be able to view their updated benefit notices beginning in late November. Those who have not enrolled in paperless notifications will receive their notices by mail during December. The personalised notices will explain the revised monthly payment, the date it takes effect and any applicable deductions. Beneficiaries enrolled in Medicare will also receive information about changes to their premiums, which can affect the amount deposited into their accounts each month. The administration said information about Medicare changes for 2027 would be available through the official Medicare website. The 3.6 per cent adjustment is higher than the 2.8 per cent increase implemented for 2026, reflecting changes in consumer prices over the relevant measurement period. The annual adjustment is calculated using the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers, compiled by the Department of Labor's Bureau of Labor Statistics. The increase is automatic under federal law and does not require separate congressional approval. The Social Security Administration also announced changes to several earnings-related thresholds for 2027. The maximum annual earnings subject to Social Security payroll taxes will increase from $184,500 to $192,300. For beneficiaries below full retirement age who continue working, the annual earnings limit before benefit withholding begins will rise from $24,480 to $25,560. The increase will also be relevant to eligible Indian-American retirees and other beneficiaries of Indian origin who receive US Social Security payments. Eligibility and payment amounts depend on individual contribution records and programme rules, rather than nationality alone.

news.title: New White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia ‘did not pass bar exam’
news.text:
By JAMES GORDON, US NEWS REPORTER 03:02 15 Oct 2026, updated 03:36 15 Oct 2026

President Donald Trump’s new White House press secretary Katie Zacharia failed the California bar exam and has never passed one in the United States, despite repeatedly describing herself as a lawyer and being introduced by the president as an attorney.

The revelation has sparked fresh questions about the legal credentials of Trump’s latest high-profile appointment, whose professional history includes working at a prestigious Chinese law firm and serving as general counsel for a political nonprofit.

Zacharia, who graduated from Pepperdine University’s law school in 2011, sat for the California bar exam shortly afterward but failed, a person with direct knowledge of the matter told The Wall Street Journal.

She was preparing for her wedding and an international move to China with her future husband at the time, according to the source.

Despite never passing an American bar examination, Zacharia went on to build a career involving international legal transactions and regularly presented herself as a lawyer during television appearances.

Her credentials have now come under intense scrutiny after searches of attorney licensing records in California, Texas and Washington, D.C., failed to identify her as a registered attorney under either her married or maiden name.

The controversy intensified when progressive journalist Judd Legum raised questions about her professional qualifications in his Popular Information newsletter.

And when Zacharia was directly questioned by a reporter on Tuesday about which state had admitted her to the bar, her response did little to clear up the mystery.

‘When I moved to China,’ she replied, without providing any further explanation.

‘I practiced international transaction law, with all the appropriate credentials,’ Zacharia said in a statement this week.

On Wednesday evening, she spoke with The New York Times in an attempt to explain her answer.

‘I assumed the question was, “Where were you after law school?”‘ she said.

‘That’s all I could hear over the sound of Marine One, and wanting to respect protocol, the distance behind the president, kept me from moving closer to hear the question,’ she went on.

In a separate statement this week, Zacharia defended her professional background.

‘I practiced international transaction law, with all the appropriate credentials,’ she insisted.

The White House has also rallied behind its new press secretary, dismissing concerns about her suitability for the prominent communications role.

‘Katie is a fabulous and wonderful addition to the team,’ White House spokesman Steven Cheung declared.

‘She is uniquely qualified and whip smart to help inform the American people about all the great things President Trump and his Administration have been doing, and she will do an incredible job as Press Secretary.’

A White House official stressed that Trump had not appointed Zacharia to perform legal work.

The distinction is significant because the press secretary’s responsibilities involve communicating administration policy and answering questions from journalists rather than providing legal advice.

Nevertheless, questions remain about Zacharia’s previous use of the title ‘lawyer’ and the nature of her professional qualifications.

After graduating from Pepperdine, Zacharia relocated to Beijing in the summer of 2011 and joined Zhong Lun Law Firm, one of China’s prominent legal practices.

There, she worked on international business transactions involving American and multinational corporations operating in China.

A person familiar with her employment told the Journal that Zacharia was among four international associates responsible for preparing agreements worth millions of dollars and communicating with corporate clients.

Crucially, the source explained that employees in the firm’s international division were classified as international legal consultants and were not required to hold Chinese attorney licenses.

American bar admission was also unnecessary for those particular duties because formal legal opinions were handled by licensed Chinese partners.

Zacharia was reportedly advised by other lawyers that her law degree and experience in international transactions qualified her to conduct legal analysis.

She also previously claimed to have worked as outside counsel to the International Finance Corporation and the World Bank while living in China.

That assertion came during a February 2025 appearance on The Clay Travis and Buck Sexton Show.

But the distinction between possessing a law degree and being licensed to practice law has become central to the growing controversy.

In the United States, attorneys generally must obtain admission to the bar in the jurisdiction where they practice, typically after passing an examination and satisfying character requirements.

news.title: Russian diesel expected to reach US market within two weeks — media
news.text:
NEW YORK, October 15. /TASS/. The United States expects that Russian diesel will reach the American market within the next two weeks, the New York Post reported, citing sources.

The fuel "should be here in the next two weeks if we get everything done," one source said, adding that Russia agreed to supply "a pretty substantial" amount. Thus, according to the newspaper, Russian diesel is expected on the US market before the November 3 midterm election.

Russian President Vladimir Putin and US President Donald Trump held a phone call on October 9, during which they discussed, among other things, petroleum product supplies. The Russian president said that Moscow had reiterated its readiness to supply oil and petroleum products to the United States and global markets. According to Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak, Russia will lift its ban on diesel exports ahead of schedule and is ready to supply 300,000 tons of diesel in October, increasing the volume to 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons in December. Monthly supplies could subsequently reach 3 million tons. The US administration, in turn, issued a general license authorizing Russian diesel supplies to the global market until April 7, 2027.

news.title: Tiffany Trump puts on leggy display in backless white minidress for 33rd birthday – inside the decadent celebration
news.text:
LEAVE A COMMENT Tiffany Trump showcased her svelte figure in an ivory minidress for her 33rd birthday, which was attended by friends and family, including her husband, Michael Boulos, and her mother, Marla Maples.

The 33-year-old was the star of the show in the minidress, which featured a tiered skirt, a beaded, sparkling bodice and a tie at the back. She completed the look with pointed heels, dangling earrings and a necklace, and wore her blonde locks down in waves.

Tiffany was surrounded by her loved ones as she blew out the candles on a large, tiered pink cake adorned with red ribbons. The restaurant that hosted her celebration was decorated with pink, red and white balloons that floated on the ceiling.

Michael stood beside her as she blew out the candles, dressed in an all-black look, while Marla took photos, sporting a silk top and pink pants. Tiffany's new sister-in-law, Bettina Anderson, who married Donald Trump Jr. in May, shared an embrace with her while wearing a lime-green strapless minidress with a white bodice.

The guest of honor was Tiffany's young son, Alexander, whom she welcomed with Michael in May 2025. Marla shared a behind-the-scenes snap of her helping Alexander get ready before the party, which Tiffany shared on her Instagram stories.

"Pre-birthday party fun with Tiffany and Alexander," she captioned the snap. Notably absent from the big bash were Tiffany's siblings, Ivanka, Donald Jr., Eric and Barron, as well as her father, Donald Trump.

Tiffany was born after Donald's divorce from his first wife, Ivana Trump, the mother of his three eldest children.

Her mother, Marla, left New York after her divorce from the businessman in 1999. "She moved us out of New York to get out of the spotlight and let me grow up and find my own identity versus being in the shadow of a name or growing up very young with all that pressure," Tiffany told People.

"So, she wanted me to have a chance to have a normal childhood. As normal as possible. I think that she did well in that." The Georgetown University alum added that despite the speculation about her distant relationship with her father, they were in fact very close and talked frequently.

"We see each other as much as possible, and of course we speak on the phone. I think regardless of distance, I don't think that dictates any relationship strains," she explained.

"I really have an emotional bond with him, and he was always just the funniest, most loving father. I'm so lucky to have parents who are so supportive of me, of each other. That really shows the respect two people have for each other."

Marla told the outlet that she wanted Tiffany to grow up close to her half-siblings and forge a strong bond with them. "I never let her ever think of them as her half-sister or half-brothers. This is your family. It was really important to me: Every birthday, every occasion, always say hi and connect."

"No matter what may have been going on between her father and [me], I wanted the kids to always stay connected and rooted," the former model said.

"I'll always love them. I knew them when they were so young, and I'm so proud of who they are today. They're all fantastic to Tiffany."

news.title: Trump suggests those who leak government information should ‘be shot’  - Jamaica Inquirer – Daily Jamaica News
news.text:
United States President Donald Trump has suggested that those who leak information to the news media should be shot as punishment.

Trump made the remarks at a campaign rally in Bullhead City, Arizona, as he urged supporters to vote in the November 3 midterm elections.

“In my opinion, leakers should be shot,” Trump told the crowd. “In the old days, we used to shoot leakers, you know, when they leak what time you’re going to attack a country.”

Trump made the statement in an apparent reference to Operation Midnight Hammer, which saw the US launch a surprise attack on Iran in June 2025 during the 12-day war between Israel and Iran.

In the aftermath of the attack, several media outlets published findings from a preliminary report by the US Defense Intelligence Agency.

That report – which had not yet been released to the public – indicated that Iran was able to move some of its enriched uranium away from the sites the US had bombed.

It also suggested that the extent of the damage to Iran’s nuclear facilities was more modest than what Trump had asserted.

Trump, however, appeared to signal that the timing of the US attacks was among the leaked information. He accused the news media of putting military members in danger, calling out The New York Times and CNN in particular.

“They leaked the time we were leaving, the time we were arriving,” Trump said, claiming he had to reschedule the bombing campaign two days later as a result.

“Somebody leaked. Some sleaze-bag, they ought to go to jail or be shot. For the rest of their life, they should be in jail.”

Trump has long had an adversarial relationship with the news media, and he has previously called for harsh punishment against any official who passes on confidential information to news outlets.

After parts of the Defense Intelligence Agency report became public, he blamed lawmakers in the Democratic Party for its release.

“The Democrats are the ones who leaked the information on the PERFECT FLIGHT to the Nuclear Sites in Iran,” Trump wrote on social media at the time. “They should be prosecuted!”

Under Trump, the White House has taken aggressive action to track down the source of leaks.

Staff in his administration, as well as officers in the military, have also been asked to take polygraph tests.

Journalists at several news outlets, including The New York Times, The Washington Post and The Wall Street Journal, have also received subpoenas aimed at determining the sources of internal information made public.

The newspapers had reported on stories such as a botched Navy SEALs raid in North Korea and how Trump ignored internal Pentagon warnings against launching the Iran war.

Last year, the Department of Defense demanded that journalists who wished to access the Pentagon sign an agreement not to publish unauthorised material.

Much of the Pentagon press corps refused to agree, and a federal court struck down many of the new demands made on journalists at the department.

Trump has long raged against leakers, going back to his first term as president from 2017 to 2021.

Former White House official Alyssa Farah Griffin told a podcast in 2024 that Trump had called for leakers to be executed, after media outlets reported that he had taken shelter in a White House bunker during racial justice protests in 2020.

Trump appeared to reprise that sentiment in his speech to Arizona voters on Wednesday, less than three weeks before the November 3 midterms.

“Leakers should be dealt with very, very strongly,” Trump said. “To me, they are the scum of the earth.”

news.title: White House spokesperson Katie Zacharia’s law career faces scrutiny  - Jamaica Inquirer – Daily Jamaica News
news.text:
Katie Zacharia, the new White House press secretary under United States President Donald Trump, has drawn increasing criticism over claims about her professional background.

On Wednesday, a public accountability nonprofit filed a complaint with the State Bar of California over Zacharia’s repeated claims that she was a lawyer.

If made falsely, such a claim is a crime in the state. According to Zacharia’s LinkedIn profile, she received a degree from the Pepperdine Caruso School of Law in 2011, but critics have questioned whether she received a licence to practise law, as she has suggested.

“Ms. Zacharia has represented herself as a lawyer repeatedly to buttress her reputation and credibility as a television legal commentator and now as the White House spokesperson,” Michelle Kuppersmith, the head of the Washington, DC-based Campaign for Accountability, said in a statement. “Yet it seems it was all a lie.”

Her organisation filed the complaint with California’s bar office, a regulatory agency that oversees the licensing of lawyers.

“In California, calling yourself a lawyer without a license isn’t puffery; it’s a crime,” Kuppersmith said.

“The State Bar should investigate whether Ms. Zacharia has misled the public about her credentials and hold her accountable if she has.”

Zacharia, a commentator who has appeared frequently on Fox News and Newsmax, began her term as White House press secretary on Tuesday.

In a news briefing that day, she seemed to falter and speak haltingly, sometimes having to repeat herself.

Her appearance was brief, lasting under 15 minutes. She spent much of her time at the podium thanking Trump for the opportunity and reading from a prepared statement.

“I have wanted to work for him for a very long time,” Zacharia said.

Later, she joined Trump outside the White House to speak further with reporters. When asked where she had passed the bar exam, Zacharia replied, “When I moved to China.”

The response was an apparent reference to a three-year stint in which she claims she worked at a law firm in Beijing.

A biography on the website for the pro-Trump women’s organisation Trumpettes USA Inc says she “served as outside counsel” for the World Bank and International Finance Corporation while in Beijing.

Her LinkedIn profile, meanwhile, indicates Zacharia served as an associate at the Zhong Lun Law Firm in Beijing from 2011 to 2013. More recently, from 2024 to 2025, it lists her as general counsel for Fix California, a voter rights group started by a Trump administration official.

On her Instagram profile, Zacharia describes herself as a “Wife, Mom, & Lawyer”.

But Zacharia’s assertion that she passed the bar in China has fuelled media scrutiny. China’s equivalent of the bar exam, the notoriously difficult National Unified Legal Professional Qualification Examination, can only be taken by Chinese citizens.

China has, on rare occasion, allowed foreigners to practise law in the country if they have several years of experience in their home countries first.

But that does not appear to be the case for Zacharia. According to media reports, Zacharia has not been found to be licensed as a lawyer in any state in the US.

In a statement to The Associated Press, Zacharia responded to the scrutiny by saying, “I practice international transaction law, with all the appropriate credentials.”

Since Trump’s return to office for a second term, Zacharia has spent several months as a communications adviser at the Department of Homeland Security.

Since June, she has also worked as the senior communications adviser at the Trump Media and Technology Group, which owns the Truth Social platform.
