news.title: Karl Rove tears apart Trump’s ‘troubling’ week as ‘things went south’ for GOP
news.text:
A veteran Republican strategist who built two winning presidential campaigns warned the GOP is stumbling into the final stretch before the midterms.

Karl Rove, a former senior adviser and deputy chief of staff to President George W. Bush, wrote in a Wednesday op-ed for The Wall Street Journal that President Donald Trump's messaging over the past week did almost nothing to sway undecided voters. After a modest start, Rove wrote, "things went south."

Rove noted the week opened with Trump's October 5 executive order allowing long-haul truckers to use dyed diesel, a fuel exempt from the federal highway tax that's meant for farm equipment and home heating. The move "sounded good to the untrained ear," he wrote, but distributors have already promised most of it to their regular farm and ranch customers.

What came next was "troubling," Rove wrote. Trump's two top political operatives traveled to Bosnia and Herzegovina to consult for a Kremlin-backed party in the breakaway region of Republika Srpska. Rove noted that U.S. consultants usually take foreign work in the off-season, "not in the final days of a crucial American campaign."

He also cited The Journal's report that Kimberly Guilfoyle, Trump's pick for ambassador to Greece, asked a Republican donor to pay off $100,000 on her American Express card just before her July 2025 Senate confirmation hearing. She resigned from the post this week.

Rove then pointed to the Pentagon's announcement that the 2009 Fort Hood shooter would be executed by firing squad on a livestream, and the Trump administration's halt on green-card applications for eight tech companies, including Microsoft and Adobe. Vice President JD Vance accused Microsoft of replacing every worker it laid off "with one and a half foreign indentured servants."

On Friday, Trump said he would lift sanctions on Russian diesel, a move Rove wrote "may violate U.S. law," then promised on Truth Social that diesel prices would fall fast. "That's very unlikely," Rove wrote.

news.title: Diaspora group urges Trump to 'preserve' PERM green card route
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Oct 15 (IANS) The Global Organization of People of Indian Origin (GOPIO) has urged President Donald Trump to preserve the Permanent Labor Certification programme, commonly known as PERM, even as a months-old suspension of software company Cloudera emerges as a test of how long the Labor Department’s curbs on eight major tech firms could last. In a letter to the White House, GOPIO Chairman Thomas Abraham and President Prakash Shah asked the administration to “preserve the Permanent Labor Certification (PERM) program while strengthening enforcement against any abuse.” The group asked for “clear, fair, and predictable procedures”, including for those “with pending cases.” It warned that skilled talent could move to “Canada, Europe, or other countries.” The appeal follows the Department of Labor’s announcement on October 8 that it would “not accept any new or process any pending” PERM applications from eight employers: Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro, HCL, Capgemini, Microsoft and Adobe. Vice President JD Vance said that day that the suspension “is gonna last as long as it needs to.” The department announced the action at a press conference. As of October 13, it had not published a notice setting out the alleged violations, the legal authority or the duration of the suspension, according to immigration law firm Goel & Anderson. The Cloudera case offers the clearest guide to what could follow. The department suspended Cloudera from PERM for 180 days on May 12 through a written release, after a Justice Department complaint filed on April 28 alleged that the company’s PERM job advertisements pointed applicants to an email address that did not work. Cloudera has said the account was not working as intended. Goel & Anderson said the likely legal basis was a federal rule allowing suspensions of up to 180 days, after which the department decides whether to resume processing or extend the action. The Cloudera decision is expected in early November, the firm said. It also said a refusal to accept new filings could resemble debarment and might face legal challenge under the Administrative Procedure Act. No lawsuit has been reported. The suspension applies only to PERM and does not affect H-1B status, the firm said. Indian firms have played down the impact. Infosys said it did “not anticipate” a “material impact”, according to the Hindu BusinessLine. Tata Consultancy Services’ PERM applications are “in single digits”, Outlook Business reported. Wipro has said more than 80 per cent of its US staff are local hires. PERM is the first step for most employment-based green cards. Employers must show the Labor Department that no qualified US worker is available for the job at the prevailing wage. Indian nationals face some of the longest green card backlogs because of per-country caps, and Indian professionals are the largest group of H-1B workers, many of whom rely on PERM to seek permanent residency.

news.title: Democratic Icon, 80, to Boost Bid to Flip Deep Red State
news.text:
The Democratic Party is sending a veteran to the front lines.

Former President Bill Clinton, 80, will join Democratic gubernatorial candidate David Jolly at an evening interfaith event in Hollywood, Florida, next week, according to MS NOW.

Jolly, a former Republican congressman, easily won the Democratic nomination in April and is facing a heated matchup against Republican Rep. Byron Donalds to succeed Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis.

Clinton is making his first public campaign appearance only two weeks before the midterm elections, similar to how he campaigned in 2022. In the days leading up to the 2022 midterms, Clinton rallied Democrats in New York, New Jersey, and South Texas.

However, the 42nd POTUS was much busier in 2024, making dozens of appearances to support then-Vice President Kamala Harris and campaigning for multiple down-ballot Democrats.

Earlier this week, he appeared alongside Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries at a fundraiser in New York to support Democratic Rep. Jared Moskowitz. The Florida congressman is running in a newly remapped district after DeSantis signed a new congressional map into law in May.

Similar to President Donald Trump, Clinton has faced scrutiny over his relationship with convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

In February, he was brought in for a closed-door deposition by the House Oversight Committee as part of a probe into the Epstein files, which included photos of the former president alongside Epstein, his accomplice Ghislaine Maxwell, and numerous unidentified women.

Clinton insisted he did nothing wrong and had “no idea” about any of the crimes Epstein committed. He added that he saw nothing that “ever gave me pause.”

“As someone who grew up in a home with domestic abuse, not only would I not have flown on his plane if I had any inkling of what he was doing—I would have turned him in myself and led the call for justice for his crimes, not sweetheart deals,” he said in a statement shared on X at the time.

Government-released documents revealed Clinton traveled on Epstein’s private jet, nicknamed the Lolita Express, 16 times.

However, even Trump, 80, felt sympathy for his Democratic adversary.

“I don’t like seeing him deposed,” Trump said of Clinton at the time. “But they certainly went after me a lot more than that.”

Trump did not extend the same sympathy to Clinton’s wife, former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, who was also deposed the day before her husband.

news.title: Tiffany Trump showcases svelte figure in backless minidress amid lavish celebration
news.text:
Tiffany Trump showcased her svelte figure in an ivory minidress for her 33rd birthday, which was attended by friends and family, including her husband, Michael Boulos, and her mother, Marla Maples.

The 33-year-old was the star of the show in the minidress, which featured a tiered skirt, a beaded, sparkling bodice and a tie at the back. She completed the look with pointed heels, dangling earrings and a necklace, and wore her blonde locks down in waves.

Inside Tiffany Trump's birthday celebration

Tiffany was surrounded by her loved ones as she blew out the candles on a large, tiered pink cake adorned with red ribbons. The restaurant that hosted her celebration was decorated with pink, red and white balloons that floated on the ceiling.

Michael stood beside her as she blew out the candles, dressed in an all-black look, while Marla took photos, sporting a silk top and pink pants. Tiffany's new sister-in-law, Bettina Anderson, who married Donald Trump Jr. in May, shared an embrace with her while wearing a lime-green strapless minidress with a white bodice.

The guest of honor was Tiffany's young son, Alexander, whom she welcomed with Michael in May 2025. Marla shared a behind-the-scenes snap of her helping Alexander get ready before the party, which Tiffany shared on her Instagram stories. 

"Pre-birthday party fun with Tiffany and Alexander," she captioned the snap. Notably absent from the big bash were Tiffany's siblings, Ivanka, Donald Jr., Eric and Barron, as well as her father, Donald Trump. 

Is Tiffany Trump close to her family?

Tiffany was born after Donald's divorce from his first wife, Ivana Trump, the mother of his three eldest children.

Her mother, Marla, left New York after her divorce from the businessman in 1999. "She moved us out of New York to get out of the spotlight and let me grow up and find my own identity versus being in the shadow of a name or growing up very young with all that pressure," Tiffany told People.

"So, she wanted me to have a chance to have a normal childhood. As normal as possible. I think that she did well in that." The Georgetown University alum added that despite the speculation about her distant relationship with her father, they were in fact very close and talked frequently.

"We see each other as much as possible, and of course we speak on the phone. I think regardless of distance, I don't think that dictates any relationship strains," she explained.

"I really have an emotional bond with him, and he was always just the funniest, most loving father. I'm so lucky to have parents who are so supportive of me, of each other. That really shows the respect two people have for each other."

Marla told the outlet that she wanted Tiffany to grow up close to her half-siblings and forge a strong bond with them. "I never let her ever think of them as her half-sister or half-brothers. This is your family. It was really important to me: Every birthday, every occasion, always say hi and connect."

"No matter what may have been going on between her father and [me], I wanted the kids to always stay connected and rooted," the former model said.

"I'll always love them. I knew them when they were so young, and I'm so proud of who they are today. They're all fantastic to Tiffany."

news.title: Britain sends £17m to Chernobyl nuclear plant hit by Russian drone attack for repairs
news.text: Andy Burnham is dispatching £17 million to a Chernobyl power plant struck by a Russian drone assault, it has been revealed. Britain will bankroll vital repairs to the facility as the PM looked to strengthen backing for Ukraine during "dark and difficult days" for the battle-scarred nation. The funds that Britain is supplying will reportedly assist in restoring its protective shelter and ventilation systems, which sustained damage during an attack last year. This comes alongside fears that deterioration could spark longer-term environmental and safety hazards. Chancellor John Healey declared the Government's dedication to the Ukrainian people was "unshakeable", while Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband stated Britain will "stand shoulder to shoulder with Ukraine and will do so until they prevail". This follows the Prime Minister welcoming Volodymyr Zelensky to Downing Street on Wednesday, October 14 when he assured the Ukrainian president the UK was "behind you and that will not change". Mr Zelensky was granted an extraordinary honour guard comprising troops from the Irish Guards upon his arrival at No 10. The encounter occurred during a spell of tense relations between Ukraine and the US after Donald Trump relaxed sanctions on Russian diesel last week as soaring fuel costs in America risked eclipsing November's mid-term elections. The UK reacted to reports of the arrangement by vowing to "maintain pressure on Russia ". In recent days, the US president has also suggested Ukraine needs a new leader and claimed Russian leader Vladimir Putin wants a peace deal more than the government in Kyiv. Mr Zelensky has also said use of Elon Musk's Starlink satellite communications system was "blocked" and that as a result "people will die", admitting that he felt betrayed by Mr Trump. "It's a pity that we are losing, we are losing a strong partner," he told Piers Morgan Uncensored. Starlink is used by Ukraine to defend against aerial attacks and for long-range drones targeting Russian sites. Speaking in the Commons ahead of his meeting with Mr Zelensky, the Prime Minister said he would seek to restore Donald Trump's support for Ukraine. During Prime Minister's Questions, Mr Burnham said he was being "careful" in his language after Mr Trump's diesel deal with Russia, as he said he was "laying the ground" for a reconciliation. He added: "I will listen to President Zelensky carefully, but he won't be going away from Britain today empty-handed." During his meeting with Mr Zelensky, he confirmed that the UK would accelerate the supply of crucial air defence missiles to Ukraine amid "heavy bombardment" from Russia. The accelerated support will see faster deliveries of British lightweight multi-role missiles to Ukraine, which have proved effective against Russian jet-powered drones. Russia continues to batter Ukraine's power grid, along with oil and gas infrastructure, despite Mr Trump's claims that both nations had reached an "energy ceasefire". Unveiling fresh funding for Chernobyl repairs, Mr Healey declared: "As the full-scale invasion of Ukraine by Putin continues, our commitment to the Ukrainian people is unshakeable. "We are curtailing the war chest funding Putin so desperately wants and backing the reconstruction of Ukraine that has suffered at the hands of his barbaric attacks." Mr Miliband stated: "Our message to Putin is clear - we stand shoulder to shoulder with Ukraine and will do so until they prevail. "Working with our allies, we are strengthening Ukraine's security, raising the cost of Russia's aggression and working towards a just and lasting peace."
news.summary: Britain will send £17 million to fund critical repairs to the Chernobyl nuclear power plant after it was hit by a Russian drone attack last year, the UK Government has announced

news.title: Iran war will end very soon, says Trump
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Oct 15 (IANS) US President Donald Trump has said the war with Iran will end very soon, predicting a rapid fall in global energy prices once the conflict is over and insisting that Tehran will not be allowed to acquire nuclear weapons. Speaking to reporters before departing Arizona for an election rally in Montana, Trump linked the expected end of the conflict to lower oil prices and improvements in the American economy. "And Iran will end very shortly. It's gonna be over very shortly, and your energy prices will fall very rapidly, very fast," Trump said. The President did not give a specific timetable for ending the conflict or explain whether negotiations were underway to secure an agreement with Tehran. He maintained that the United States had achieved its central military objective of preventing Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons. "And I had to make an excursion down to Iran to take away the nuclear weapon. And we've done that. They won't have a nuclear weapon," he said. Trump repeated the assurance moments later. "Uh, the war's gonna be over very soon. Thank you very much." His remarks came after a campaign rally in Bullhead City, Arizona, where he gave a more detailed account of the American military campaign against Iran and its consequences for international energy markets. At that rally, Trump claimed that American military operations had severely weakened Iran's armed forces, including its naval and air capabilities. He also suggested that the scale of the operations had complicated Washington's ability to identify Iranian officials with whom it could negotiate. "I might have gone too far. I don't know who the hell to deal with," Trump said while discussing the removal of successive levels of Iranian leadership. The President said the United States had established control over the Strait of Hormuz, a crucial maritime passage for international oil shipments. He claimed that oil movements through the waterway had recovered despite the military confrontation. "But, you know, we have taken total control of the Hormuz Strait, and we're taking more gasoline -- we're taking more oil right now out of the Hormuz Strait than we did before this started," he said. Trump attributed the situation to American naval operations, including a blockade that he described as a wall of steel. He argued that preventing Iran from obtaining nuclear weapons justified the economic consequences of military action. The President also addressed inflation after being asked whether he had discussed the latest inflation report with Kevin Warsh. "We're at 1.7 per cent inflation for the last three months," he said, describing the administration's economic performance as strong. He compared current oil prices with those during former President Joe Biden's administration and argued that energy remained cheaper despite the confrontation with Iran. Trump did not directly address the question about market expectations of an interest rate increase. The Strait of Hormuz connects the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea. It is one of the world's most strategically important maritime routes for crude oil and liquefied natural gas shipments.

news.text:
President Donald Trump's newly installed press secretary has long presented herself as a lawyer, but a bombshell report raises serious doubts about that claim.

Katie Zacharia never passed a bar exam in the United States, The Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday. She took the California bar after finishing law school at Pepperdine University in 2011 and failed it, according to a source with direct knowledge cited by The Journal.

Trump described Zacharia as an attorney when he tapped her for the White House podium. Questions about her credentials began circulating after she turned up in no searches of licensed attorneys in California, Texas or Washington, D.C., under either her married or maiden name. Journalist Judd Legum had flagged the issue in his Popular Information newsletter.

Zacharia offered little clarity when a reporter asked her Tuesday what state she had passed the bar in. "When I moved to China," she answered, and left it there.

She insisted in a statement, "I practiced international transaction law, with all the appropriate credentials."

After the exam, Zacharia relocated to Beijing to work for Zhong Lun Law Firm. A person familiar with her time there told The Journal that international staff at the firm were considered legal consultants and did not need a Chinese license, since local partners handled formal legal opinions.

Still, Zacharia routinely described herself as a lawyer on cable news. Weighing in on the trial of Charlie Kirk's accused killer during an August 31 Fox News segment, she said, "As a lawyer, the procedural steps are absolutely critical to ensure that they get this right." The network's on-screen graphic labeled her an attorney.

The distinction carries real weight. Practicing law in the U.S. requires a license from the relevant jurisdiction, and some states can bring criminal charges against people who pass themselves off as attorneys without bar admission.

Roger Alford, a Notre Dame law professor who employed Zacharia as a research assistant at Pepperdine, praised her as "a star" but acknowledged that "generally speaking it would be unusual to say that you're a lawyer if you've not passed the bar somewhere."

The White House rallied behind her. Spokesman Steven Cheung called Zacharia "uniquely qualified and whip smart," while a Trump administration official stressed that Trump did not bring her on to handle legal work.

Elon Musk’s apparent decision, likely at Donald Trump’s behest, to limit Ukraine Starlink in the middle of its existential war with Russia, is going to be the last straw for many nations looking to not just Starlink, but anything this man has decision-making powers over. It has laid bare, for all to see, the national security risk of outsourcing crucial capabilities to a wayward and unpredictable trillionaire.

For quite some time now, Elon Musk has been visibly heading towards one of the oldest and most predictable outcomes for any person who assumes wealth and power are all that matters. Namely, forgetting that power comes in many forms, not all of which are linked to wealth, and many of which have no relationship to it at all. Prominent among these is the natural desire of human beings to live safely.

By agreeing to a Trump Administration demand, Musk has now shown not only that he will bargain away the lives of Ukrainian civilians in exchange for continued favor with the mighty, but that in his cost-benefit calculation human lives come out on the short end. In other words, faced with the choice between more dead Ukrainian civilians and being fenced out of the access to Trump he needs in order to grow even more rich and powerful himself, he chose more dead Ukrainian civilians.

The Polish Foreign Minister already fired the first shot across Elon’s bow yesterday, warning him that not only his Polish customer (who pays for Ukraine’s access) but all of his European customers, are watching. What value are national security contracts with companies run by a man who will violate them at his whim for his other perceived interests? I realize this sort of thing can happen in business, but rarely when it so obviously leads predictably high mass casualties of innocents.

The scenarios write themselves. Russia decides to initiate conflict with NATO by sending soldiers in unmarked uniforms into Estonia. NATO decides to retaliate, but suddenly discovers its Starlink services have been cut off. NATO soldiers and Estonian civilians die. It turns out Putin made a few phone calls. Or China decides to take Taiwan and Taiwan defenses get overwhelmed as Starlink goes down after China’s leader hits the speed dial to Musk.

There is a larger lesson here of course, one often made by Sen. Bernie Sanders (D-VT) and many others – that allowing such concentrations of wealth pose not just issues of economic fairness, but real national security risks. In a sense, Elon Musk is doing everyone a favor. He is illustrating Bernie’s arguments.

Far from being a genius, Musk has shown on numerous occasions that his mindset has evolved into megalomania. He is taking what used to be a humorous saying – that at a certain point great wealth turns into “F U money” (meaning one can buy oneself out of or into any situation) literally. He should have already learned lessons from his unsuccessful attempt to buy state supreme court elections a year or so ago. He will learn more November 3, as his quarter of a billion burns in an failed attempt to keep GOP control of the US Congress.

The pushback has already begun. And it won’t stop. Elon’s actions won’t be forgotten. Ukraine and its allies, as they watch Ukrainian men, women and children get buried under Russian drones and missiles, won’t let them be. It adds to the pile that includes the destruction of USAID (and the thousands of lives lost in developing countries thereby).

The Big Man (as the Polish Minister called him), will learn what others of his like found out all through recorded history. Something that used to be whispered into the ears of a new Caesar of Rome every time he took power.

news.title: Trump just gave the one rant that all Republicans should be confronted with: Jen Psaki
news.text:
MS NOW's Jen Psaki challenged the media to nail every last Republican running for re-election on a particular rant President Donald Trump ushered forth on Wednesday in Arizona.

"Today, Donald Trump delivered what I would consider his most unhinged performance at a political rally I have seen to date," said Psaki. "Look, I understand how easy it is to dismiss whatever nonsense falls out of Trump's mouth on a given day, right? The nonsense is, after all, part of the strategy."

That is why, Psaki said, MS NOW generally ignores his rallies and doesn't give them any more oxygen than they need: "Because so often the noise is just that it's noise. But tonight is not one of those times."

Now, she said, "I happen to think that every single Republican in every single race in the country should have to answer for the things Donald Trump is saying right now." And in particular, she said, they should be pressed on "a range of things that Trump said in Bullhead City, Arizona, today, including what he said in an apparent reference to the first strikes Trump ordered on Iran this summer ... and the subsequent reporting that came out of the Pentagon."

"Somebody leaked, some sleazebag," said Trump in the clip. "They ought to go to jail and be shot for the rest of their life. They should be in jail. Leakers should be — in my opinion, leakers should be shot. They should be shot. In the old days, we used to shoot leakers. You know, leakers should be dealt with very, very strongly. They're real to me. They're the scum of the Earth!"

"This is not the most important detail, but there were no leaks before the first strikes on Iran," Psaki noted. But more to the point, "Donald Trump says leakers should be shot."

"Every Republican candidate should be asked between now and November ... do you agree with Donald Trump that leakers should be shot?" said Psaki. "Everybody should be asked that question. Do you agree with Donald Trump that the U.S. government should shoot anyone who leaks information to the media?" 

It could be "a simple yes or no," she added, but "the leader of your party thinks they should be. Do you agree?"

news.title: 'Big Bang Theory' Producer Chuck Lorre: A Society that Abandons God will Turn to Communism
news.text:
Hollywood producer Chuck Lorre — known for being behind popular sh0ws like The Big Bang Theory and Two and a Half Men — said societies that abandon God end up turning toward tyranny.

“When civilizations or cultures took God out of the picture, they replaced it with a Communist party, with a fascist dictator,” Lorre said during his appearance on Tuesday’s episode of The Joe Rogan Experience.

“It’s the same idea: ‘Organize around me. It doesn’t matter if I’m right or not, organize around me.’ And people will,” the producer warned. “And if you take that away from them, they get angry.”

“It freaks them out,” Lorre added. “Because it’s like the tent pole. That tent pole moves, the tent comes down and everything, you know, if you believe that this is the truth and someone says, ‘No, it’s not. It’s bullshit,’ everything else you believe is in fair play. Everything.”

Elsewhere in their discussion, the Hollywood producer told Rogan that “as glorious” as “fame and adulation and fancy cars” are, such worldly entities are “not the real solution.”

“The real solution — I’m going to say it and then regret it — but the real solution is a spiritual solution. You have to find something beyond this world,” he said.

Rogan then chimed in, asking, “Why would you regret saying that?” before inquiring with a laugh: “Because you live in L.A.? Because you’re in your bubble?”

The Young Sheldon producer responded by stating that he didn’t want to be associated with “new age bullshit.”

“But I don’t know any other way,” Lorre added. “And I do know that in my own life, seeking a spiritual illusion — not finding it, but the act of seeking it — there’s some salvation in that.”

Rogan agreed, adding, “I don’t think there’s anything silly about it.”

“And I think the problem is, the term has been co-opted,” the podcast host continued. “The term ‘spirituality’ has been co-opted by people that you do consider to be flaky. That’s the problem.”

Lorre agreed, adding that he believes other people have given “spirituality” a “bad name.”

Notably, the Hollywood producer is also no stranger to attempting to give others a bad name.

Last month, Lorre called First Lady Melania Trump a “Yugoslavian escort” during his acceptance speech at a charity gala in Los Angeles. He also called President Donald Trump a “Russian asset” and joked about the idea of the president having a heart attack.

The White House responded by advising that Lorre “seek psychiatric help.”

news.title: North Korea says it tested cruise missiles designed to be fired from submarines
news.text:
North Korea says it has test-fired cruise missiles designed to be fired from submarines as it continues to expand its military capabilities during a prolonged freeze in diplomacy with Washington and Seoul.

North Korean state media on Thursday said the military tested two types of such missiles in the country’s eastern waters on Wednesday. The report described the weapons as strategic, implying an intent to arm them with nuclear warheads, but did not specify whether they were launched from an actual submarine or an underwater test platform.

North Korean state media said the tests were aimed at assessing the readiness of the country’s underwater combat systems, improving the Navy’s ability to carry out strategic missions and demonstrating the reliability of its nuclear deterrent.

The South’s military did not immediately comment on the tests.

The launches extended a recent run in weapons demonstrations, including tests of various hypersonic missile systems on Sept. 20 and Oct. 3 that the North said were aimed at advancing its arsenal of weapons designed to overwhelm missile defenses in South Korea and Japan.

North Korea for years has been developing various ballistic and cruise missiles designed to be fired from underwater. It has also claimed progress in recent months in building a nuclear-powered submarine that it intends to arm with nuclear-capable weapons, as leader Kim Jong Un turns his focus to strengthening the navy after a decade of expanding the country’s ballistic missile program. 

North Korea’s potential acquisition of a submarine capable of operating stealthily for extended periods and launching missiles from underwater would be a worrying development for its neighbors as such launches would be difficult to detect in advance. But there have been questions about whether North Korea, a heavily sanctioned and impoverished country, has the resources and technology needed to build such systems.

North Korea in recent weeks has also conducted live-fire drills and commissioned a new warship as leader Kim Jong Un continues to flaunt his nuclear weapons program while rejecting U.S. and South Korean offers to resume long-stalled diplomacy.

Kim in recent years has halted all diplomacy and cooperation with South Korea and described it as a permanent enemy amid a yearslong stalemate in larger nuclear negotiations with Washington. 

He has so far rebuffed U.S. President Donald Trump’s calls to revive their diplomacy, which broke down in 2019. His government has called for Washington to abandon its “hostile” policy toward Pyongyang and drop demands for North Korea’s denuclearization as a precondition for talks.
news.summary: North Korea says it has test-fired cruise missiles designed for submarines, continuing to expand its military capabilities amid a diplomatic freeze with Washington and Seoul

Hello, this is Hui Jie writing to you from Singapore. Welcome to another edition of CNBC's Daily Open.

Tensions in the Strait of Hormuz have risen after a Singapore registered ship was sunk in the critical waterway, and Iran said it was "counting the moments" until it can strike U.S. warships.

Oil markets responded to mounting worries, with prices of the critical commodity extending gains, while U.S. President Donald Trump's deal with Russia for supplying diesel is unlikely to materially impact prices.

A major escalation in the Strait of Hormuz has seen a container ship sunk in the waterway, as Iran escalated its attacks on commercial vessels.

The GFS Pride, registered in Singapore, sank after it was struck by an unidentified projectile and caught fire. The ship's 21 crew members were safely evacuated and no injuries were reported, according to the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore.

"Such attacks are unprovoked, unjustifiable and a breach of international law," the Singapore maritime authority said in a statement Wednesday.

A second vessel, the GFS Giselle, was also hit and sustained damage to its hull, but managed to arrive at safe anchorage and none of its crew were hurt, the authority added.

Tehran has also ratcheted up its rhetoric, saying it was ‘counting the moments’ until it can strike U.S. warships in the Strait.

Islamic Revolutionary Guard chief Ali Ozmaei reportedly said Wednesday, "If the Americans think the Strait of Hormuz is open, let them come closer. We are impatient to sink American warships."

Washington's forces, however, disputed the claims of Iranian control, with U.S. Central Command saying "American forces and regional partners clearly control the Strait of Hormuz."

The recent development, along with additional attacks by Tehran-backed Houthi rebels on oil giant Saudi Aramco's facilities in Saudi Arabia, have pushed oil prices higher, with international benchmark Brent up at $106.06 a barrel, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate advanced to $95.09 a barrel.

High energy prices have also contributed to a hot inflation report in the U.S., with the consumer inflation rate for September up 3.7% year on year, higher than expectations of 3.6%.

The energy index jumped 5.2% as tensions continued between the U.S. and Iran in a war launched in late February that shows no signs of ending anytime soon.

Core CPI — which strips out prices of food and energy — was up 2.6% on an annual basis, compared with estimates of 2.5%.

Markets slipped on the news, with the S&P 500 pulling back 1.11% and the Nasdaq Composite shed 1.88%. Tracking Wall Street declines overnight, Asia markets tumbled Thursday.

The CPI report comes as oil prices remain elevated and consumers pay more for gasoline, which is averaging at $4.33 a gallon, compared to about $3.08 per gallon a year earlier, according to AAA.

Last week, Trump announced he would temporarily ease restrictions on Russian diesel fuel exports, but analysts don't believe the deal will do much to lower fuel prices for truckers and farmers.

Over in the tech world, trouble is also brewing as Netflix said on Wednesday it will lay off roughly 6% of its employees, or about 1,000 workers, according to a memo obtained by CNBC.

The job cuts will largely impact the product, tech, legal and HR teams. The layoffs come just a few weeks after Sarandos told attendees at the Bloomberg Screentime conference that the company was "not growing as fast as I want."

AI giant OpenAI is also facing a legal quagmire of its own, with eight U.S. states filing lawsuits against the company on Wednesday.

The suit alleges that the artificial intelligence company's ChatGPT chatbot is an unsafe product that's harmed children and deceived parents.

Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird said in a release that "OpenAI claims ChatGPT is safe while it's giving dangerous medical advice, encouraging people to hurt others, and coaching people to commit suicide — all while pretending to be their fake friend," she added.

G20 finance ministers and central bank governors are meeting on the sidelines of the IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok on Thursday, although U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent will be skipping the event.

The U.S. holds this year's G20 presidency, and the question would be how much gets done before leaders convene again in Miami in December.

Scott Bessent’s growth plans aren’t enough to tame surging deficit and debt pile, IMF chief says

The head of the International Monetary Fund has urged Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to trim the deficit, warning that his plan to lean on growth to tame U.S. Government debt isn't sufficient.

"Growth of course helps, but it cannot deliver fast enough the necessary adjustments," Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said at a panel Wednesday at the IMF-World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok. "Some [fiscal] measures would be necessary."

Georgieva said Bessent recognizes that federal deficits and overall debt have grown "too high," and that measures to improve the budget balance and reduce the debt are necessary. But "the authorities very much rely on strong growth in the United States" to bring them down, she said.

news.title: Inquest into death of man killed by tiger at wildlife park to be opened
news.text:
An inquest into the death of a man who was killed by a tiger after entering its enclosure at a wildlife park is set to open on Thursday.

William Chapman, 23, was mauled to death by the animal at Yorkshire Wildlife Park, in Doncaster, on Saturday.

A hearing is scheduled at Doncaster Coroner’s Court at 10am on Thursday.

Former child actor Mr Chapman’s family said he had suffered from “significant mental illness over a number of years” and was “prescribed strong medication”.

In a statement released on Tuesday evening, they said: “It will be for the coroner to decide what part this played in his death.

“We would ask everybody to respect that process.”

Mr Chapman’s family also said “deeply offensive media content is causing them severe distress” after US President Donald Trump reposted a widely shared video of the incident.

“The family are utterly devastated by their loss and are struggling to come to terms with what has happened,” they said.

“The publication and circulation of deeply offensive media content is causing them severe distress at an exceptionally vulnerable time. We ask people to stop doing this.

“The family are hopeful that the relevant authorities will do their upmost to get to the bottom of why our amazing son did what he did.”

They added: “William was a bright, warm and engaging young man whom his family dearly loved – and William loved them back.

As a child, Mr Chapman appeared in ITV’s May Contain Nuts, alongside Harry Potter actress Shirley Henderson, and in the BBC’s True Stories series, according to IMDB.

He previously attended Jackie Palmer Stage School in High Wycombe, Buckinghamshire.

In a tribute shared on Facebook, the school said it was “deeply saddened” to hear of the loss of its former student, adding “we loved watching William grow, both as a person and as a performer”.

Emergency services were contacted shortly after 1.30pm on October 10 when Mr Chapman, who police said was visiting the park alone, entered the enclosure.

He was pronounced dead at the scene.

City of Doncaster Council, which is responsible for licensing the park, said on Monday it had started a health and safety investigation.

Dan Swaine, executive director of place at City of Doncaster Council, said: “As the relevant licensing authority for the Yorkshire Wildlife Park, I can confirm that, in line with our statutory duties, the council has launched a health and safety investigation.”

In a previous statement on social media, the wildlife park said “many, many people” had contacted them about Altai, the Amur tiger involved in the incident, and it confirmed he is “safe and well” and will not be euthanised.
news.summary: William Chapman, 23, was mauled to death by the animal at Yorkshire Wildlife Park, in Doncaster, on Saturday

news.title: DOJ insiders spot fatal flaw in Trump White House’s revenge probe over public snub: report
news.text:
The White House helped steer a Justice Department probe into major TV networks, but some inside the department doubt it will survive.

The White House was a driving force behind the DOJ's antitrust investigation into the networks' brief suspension of pooled presidential coverage, three people familiar with the matter told Semafor on Wednesday. Some inside the DOJ question the probe's legal merits, and two former DOJ officials told Semafor the networks' move is likely shielded by the First Amendment. 

One of them cited a 1982 Supreme Court decision that extended constitutional protection to group boycotts carried out for political reasons.

The networks pulled out of the pool after three news outlets were barred from the White House.

Two of the sources indicated the idea for an antitrust inquiry originated inside the White House before officials there pushed the Justice Department to pursue it. A third source brushed off the question of who came up with it first, calling it a "distinction [without] a difference" given how tightly the two operate under President Donald Trump.

A DOJ official pushed back on that account, insisting that "seasoned attorneys within the Justice Department, including the antitrust division, first discussed this." The official also said any information requests that may have gone to networks were written "because there is sound legal footing to investigate."

The antitrust division's ties to the White House run deep, Semafor noted. Sara Matar, who previously served as the division's chief of staff, moved to the White House counsel's office in August as an associate.

White House spokesperson Lauren Bis issued a statement after Semafor's report was published. "Your sources have it wrong," she said. "As the Department of Justice said, this investigation did not initiate with the White House."

The probe also echoes a demand from MAGA activist Laura Loomer, who posted last month questioning why the DOJ hadn't "filed an antitrust lawsuit" against outlets that she said "colluded to refuse to cover" Trump. Loomer traveled with Trump to Alabama the following week, though it's not clear whether she brought up the matter with him.

Attorney General Todd Blanche has openly defended the president's right to point the DOJ toward targets, Semafor noted. Speaking at Semafor's World Economy Summit in April, Blanche said that when "the leader of the Free World" wants the DOJ to "focus on something," acting on it is "of course, what every Department of Justice has done."

Legal experts see the investigation as a possible avenue for the DOJ to obtain internal records from the networks, according to Axios.

news.title: The Great Oil Heist
news.text:
When the United States ousted Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro earlier this year and put him in a New York jail cell, Venezuelans at home and abroad rejoiced. For the first time in 27 years, the country faced a real possibility of regime change. But removing an autocrat does not necessarily dismantle the authoritarian system that kept him in power, particularly when the man who removed him is an aspiring authoritarian and kleptocrat in his own right.

Nearly nine months after Maduro’s capture by US special forces, the prospect of democratic change is dimming by the day. That was evident recently during the United Nations General Assembly, where US President Donald Trump warmly welcomed the leader he left in charge of the country, Delcy Rodríguez, who had been Maduro’s vice president. Trump’s backing has prompted several US allies in Latin America to warm to the chavista government, as seen in last month’s meeting between Paraguayan President Santiago Peña and Rodríguez.

This is happening even as the UN’s fact-finding mission on Venezuela reports that the machinery of repression built under chavismo remains largely intact. While some political prisoners have been released, and access to some previously blocked media outlets has been restored, the most recognisable figures of the Maduro regime are still in power. The security services and military high command have not been purged of regime loyalists, and armed colectivos continue to operate with impunity. No matter how US Secretary of State Marco Rubio tries to spin these facts, or how often Rodríguez promises free elections, a democratic transition is not in sight.

Trump’s priorities—energy security, access to low-cost oil, and rewarding his business cronies—help explain this authoritarian inertia. Venezuela offers all three, with its vast oil reserves providing US refineries with additional supplies and reducing exposure to energy-market instability. In August, for example, the Trump administration struck a deal with North American Blue Energy Partners, granting the company a 100-year concession to 17 Venezuelan oil fields containing roughly 65 billion barrels of proven reserves. The US government also acquired a 35% stake in the company and the right to buy 20% of its production at cost.

And more investment is on the way, as Venezuela’s interim government expects the NABEP deal alone to deliver as much as $100 billion in infrastructure investments. Chevron is expanding its Venezuelan operations, and ExxonMobil is discussing a return to the country almost two decades after Hugo Chávez nationalised its oil assets.

There is no inherent contradiction between economic recovery and democratisation. The two can and should go hand in hand, as they did in countries like Poland in the 1990s. The problem begins when economic stabilisation is put first, without a clear plan for a democratic transition—precisely the Trump administration’s approach. In his first press conference after Maduro’s capture, Trump barely mentioned democracy but had plenty to say about oil.

A 100-year concession is not an ordinary foreign investment. It assumes the basic arrangement will survive across US administrations. And since the US government has a direct stake in the company, American taxpayers have a vested interest in protecting it.

Trump’s oil deal, brokered by businessman Alejandro Betancourt, a chavista loyalist who has been implicated in multiple corruption scandals, was negotiated with little transparency and no competitive bidding by the Rodríguez government, whose constitutional legitimacy remains contested. The deal places a significant share of Venezuela’s main asset under the control of a foreign government for an extraordinary length of time. Add Trump’s declaration at the UNGA that the US should control Venezuela’s oil because “to the victor go the spoils,” and it’s easy to see why a future democratically elected Venezuelan government may want to revisit the deal.

Nothing requires American oil companies to oppose democracy or deliberately block elections, but billions of dollars in US and foreign investment create powerful incentives to avoid the uncertainty that free elections and a new government would bring. A Venezuelan government that protects contracts, keeps the oil flowing, cooperates with the US government, and allows American companies to operate freely is immensely valuable, regardless of how democratic it is.

If this deal does materialise, then those incentives will not disappear when Trump leaves office. Venezuela could end up stable enough for foreign companies to invest, yet never democratic enough to put those investments at risk. The Trump administration has already demonstrated its eagerness to work with the same repressive regime it once bitterly opposed when its interests are at stake.

Before Maduro’s removal, the impoverished chavista government was grappling with collapsing oil production and had few international partners. New oil revenues could ease some of Venezuela’s economic misery and enable the regime to rebuild relations with neighbouring countries, making it harder to dislodge.

That leaves the chavista regime with a better chance of survival, while the US gets greater energy security and a pliable ally in Caracas—a win-win for everyone but Venezuelans yearning for political freedom. Maduro’s removal created an opportunity for democratic change. Trump’s oil heist is turning it into the path not taken.

The writer is an international political analyst and lectures on comparative political economy and the political economy of corruption at King’s College London.
news.summary: When the United States ousted Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro earlier this year and put him in a New York jail cell, Venezuelans at home and abroad rejoiced. For the first time in 27 years, the country faced a real possibility of regime change. But removing an autocrat does not necessarily dismantle the authoritarian system that […]

news.title: Houthis' Missile Push: Can Chinese Components Help Replicate Iran's Kheibar Shekan?
news.text: Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis are working to build advanced ballistic missiles using components shipped from China, according to a Wall Street Journal report that cites an investigation by Conflict Armament Research (CAR).The weapons could put both Saudi Arabia and Israel within range.CAR, a group that tracks weapons and their supply chains in conflict zones, said the missiles appear to be modelled on Iran's Kheibar Shekan.The precision-guided ballistic missile can change course in flight, which makes it harder for air defence systems to intercept. A missile of this design could travel up to 1,200 miles.The findings come as Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia have intensified in recent weeks, deepening tensions over a Riyadh-led blockade. Together with Iran's continued disruption of commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, the attacks have pushed oil prices higher.US President Donald Trump has accused the Houthis of behaving "very badly" in a post on Truth Social.CAR based its report on information from Yemeni authorities, who intercepted two shipments last year and shared details with investigators in July. Missile-related equipment had been hidden among other goods.The seized items included custom-made metal parts for a missile's motor and airframe, and fins used to keep it stable in flight.ALSO READ | Riyadh Airport Under Attack: Why Saudi Arabia Is Struggling To Defeat The HouthisInvestigators also found parts linked to a solid-propellant rocket motor from the Kheibar Shekan family, along with testing equipment, tools, raw materials and heat-resistant ablative material used to shield missiles during flight.Shipping documents seen by CAR pointed to a Chinese precision-metal manufacturer that markets itself as a specialist in custom aerospace parts.The report did not name the firm. Some of the components could have civilian uses, but others appeared to be built specifically for missiles.Henry Thompson, a former member of the UN's Yemen sanctions panel, told the WSJ that evidence suggests the Houthis have been importing parts for solid-fuel ballistic missiles from China for at least two years.He said such missiles can carry bigger payloads deeper into Saudi territory than the group's cruise missiles and drones, making them a more serious threat.ALSO READ | 'Unacceptable': India Condemns 'Dastardly' Riyadh Airport Missile Strike That Killed 12Moreover, UN reports and data gathered by arms experts show Chinese companies are the largest source of seized goods bound for the Houthis, and most suppliers of drone parts sanctioned by the US for links to the group are based in China.The Houthis are under a UN arms embargo and are designated a terrorist organisation by the US. Washington accused a Chinese company last year of helping the group attack US vessels in the Red Sea.Beijing says it respects the UN ban on arms sales to the Yemeni faction.In late 2024, CAR documented imports of similar custom-machined parts linked to the shorter-range Sadr missile, though the supplier was never identified.
news.summary: The findings come as Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia have intensified in recent weeks, deepening tensions over a Riyadh-led blockade.

news.title: 'Illegal, ineffective': Trump under fire for Russia oil deal as Graham Act deadline nears
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Oct 15 (IANS) Indian-American Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi stepped up attacks on President Donald Trump's deal to buy Russian diesel, even as Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev defended it, days before a sanctions law deadline that could bring steep tariffs on major buyers of Russian oil such as India and China. "Trump started an illegal war with Iran that sent fuel prices soaring. Now he's rewarding Putin with a Russian diesel deal while pressuring Ukraine to stop striking Russian oil facilities," Krishnamoorthi wrote on X on Wednesday (local time). "Putin gets billions. Ukraine gets more Russian attacks. Americans get stuck with the bill," the Illinois Democrat added. In a later post, he said the deal "would help bankroll Putin's war machine without meaningfully lowering fuel prices for Americans". "It's illegal, ineffective, and no substitute for ending Trump's Iran war," he wrote. Dmitriev, Russian President Vladimir Putin's special envoy for investment and economic cooperation, pushed back on X. "All pragmatic world leaders who care about their people want affordable diesel, gas and oil, including from Russia," he wrote. In another post, he attacked The Economist, saying it failed to mention "the 5 per cent decline in diesel prices from the deal, showcasing its benefits to US farmers, consumers and energy markets". Dmitriev did not say how he arrived at the figure or over what period prices had fallen. Opposition on Capitol Hill has grown. Senator Richard Blumenthal, a Connecticut Democrat, said he was "leading 12 of my colleagues demanding that Trump rescind the disastrous Russian diesel deal". "It betrays American security interests & brave Ukrainians fighting Putin's bloody slaughter," he wrote. Representative James Clyburn of South Carolina called it "a mistake". "Trump's decision to ease sanctions on Russian diesel will do little to lower US fuel prices but a lot to fund Russia's war against our ally Ukraine," he wrote. Representative Greg Stanton of Arizona said the plan was "likely illegal and unlikely to lower prices", adding that it would "funnel billions of dollars into Putin's Russia". Representative Mike Levin of California called it "a lifeline for Russia's war machine", citing a New York Times estimate that around $4 billion of American money could flow into Russia's economy. The Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control issued General License 135 on Friday, authorising transactions involving Russian-origin diesel until April 2027. The dispute comes as the deadline under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 approaches on October 18. Section 113 of the law requires the President to raise duties to "up to 100 per cent" on goods from countries that were among the five largest importers of Russian crude oil or natural gas and that knowingly make new purchases after the deadline. The President can waive the duties by certifying to Congress that a waiver is in the US national interest. The administration has not said publicly how it will apply the law. New Delhi has long argued that it is held to a different standard from Western countries that continue to trade with Russia.

news.title: Tension erupts during House midterm debate as Lawler fact-checks New York Democrat opponent on immigration
news.text: Rep. Mike Lawler, R-N.Y., faced off against Democrat opponent Cait Conley Wednesday night in a one-hour debate filled with interruptions and fiery accusations less than three weeks before Election Day. Lawler is vying for a third term representing New York's 17th Congressional District, a politically moderate area in the New York City suburbs that could decide the fate of who controls the House of Representatives for the final years of President Donald Trump's term. Lawler called out Conley for misrepresenting his voting record, Trump's One Big Beautiful Bill Act and her own stance on immigration enforcement. Conley, meanwhile, tried to paint Lawler as a Trump acolyte who put the needs of Washington Republicans ahead of the people of his district. Their most heated clashes came on the immigration front, when the moderator referenced the recent shooting of an illegal immigrant by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents last week in New York City while the man's 5-year-old child was in the car. DEM CANDIDATE CLEARS CROWDED FIELD TO FACE TRUMP-BACKED INCUMBENT IN NY "I believe that border security is national security and that we do need immigration enforcement to ensure that violent criminals and drug cartels and human traffickers and terrorist organizations aren't in our communities and that they are deported," Conley said. "But what we are seeing right now with the conduct of ICE is posing a public safety hazard. To your point, last week, they shot into a car where there was a 5-year-old child. I'll tell you, as a law enforcement officer, you're not permitted to do that kind of stuff." NEW YORK GOVERNOR DEBATE HEATS UP AS BLAKEMAN, HOCHUL SPAR OVER TRUMP, SANCTUARY STATUS, ICE SHOOTING Lawler, however, pointed out the man has a lengthy criminal rap sheet and was seen by some as a danger to his community. He also argued the shooting would never have happened had local law enforcement not been barred from handing him over to ICE by New York's sanctuary laws. He said Conley "supports making New York a sanctuary state, prohibits cooperation between local law enforcement and federal immigration officials." WATCH: LAWLER UNLOADS ON RASKIN AFTER FIERY IMMIGRATION HEARING: ‘GROW THE F--- UP’ Lawler later pivoted the discussion to Sheridan Gorman, the college student from his district who was killed while out with her friends near her campus in Chicago earlier this year. The illegal immigrant accused of killing her was previously charged with shoplifting, but Chicago sanctuary laws prevent local law enforcement from handing him over to ICE. Conley called Gorman's death "an atrocious crime" while repeatedly pointing out it took place in Chicago. Lawler attempted to intervene multiple times to call it "preventable," to which an irate Conley responded, "Can I finish?" "And I do support federal agents and federal law enforcement, federal immigration enforcement, making sure that we deport violent citizens," she said. DHS BOSS REVEALS OVAL OFFICE PLAN TO 'WITHHOLD FUNDING' FROM SANCTUARY CITIES AFTER AGGRESSIVE NEW YORK BUST Lawler then argued, however, that Conley's support of sanctuary policies runs counter to that. "If you think he should have been deported when he was arrested for shoplifting, he should have been turned over to ICE. Under the new law that you support, he will not be turned over to ICE, and he will be released under cashless bail," Lawler said. It prompted the moderator to step in, telling Lawler there was no "cross-examination round." Elsewhere in the debate, Lawler accused Conley of having "literally just lied" that Lawler voted with Trump "100% of the time." 10 DEMOCRAT-HELD HOUSE SEATS REPUBLICANS COULD FLIP TO SAVE THEIR MAJORITY "I've been rated the third most independent member of my conference. And I have taken on the president on numerous issues, including lifting the cap on SALT, including extending Haitian TPS, including passing an extension for the ACA enhanced premium tax credit despite his objections," Lawler said. Earlier in the debate, Conley tried to accuse Lawler of supporting tax breaks for companies that build data centers as part of the One Big Beautiful Bill. Lawler shot back, "I know you just moved here from Virginia, so it's hard for you to understand the local communities, but the fact is ... the provision you referenced in the Working Families Tax Cut Act is $80 billion for 100% expensing for every business in America to expense plant, property and equipment. "Are you against our small businesses in the Hudson Valley being able to expense their plant, property and equipment and hire more people? Your attack on that rings hollow. You clearly don't understand what's actually in the tax bill. And part of the problem is you don't pay property taxes." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Amid the drama were moments of civility. Both candidates shook hands after their spirited debate and thanked each other for appearing. Lawler also thanked Conley for her military service. The district is a pivotal one for control of the House next year. Lawler is one of three House Republicans who won a district that former Vice President Kamala Harris also won in 2024. And in an election that's expected to be brutal for the GOP, both sides are pouring millions of dollars into the fight.
news.summary: Rep. Mike Lawler, R-N.Y., and Democrat Cait Conley clashed over ICE enforcement and New York sanctuary laws in a fiery debate that could decide House control in 2026.

news.title: White House punches back at Chicago Mayor Johnson over reparations demands
news.text:
The White House punched back at Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson Wednesday after the progressive mayor claimed President Donald Trump neglected compensation for descendants of formerly enslaved Black Americans while favoring the wealthy.

Johnson appeared on the “Native Land Pod” podcast Sunday to discuss his administration’s crime reduction efforts in Chicago, where violent crime rates have fallen sharply, according to the Johnson administration and Chicago Police Department data.

Speaking with hosts Angela Rye, Bakari Sellers and Andrew Gillum, Johnson argued that public safety “has to be something more than just policing,” highlighting city investments in “mental behavioral healthcare, promoting detectives and expanding and investing in CVI (community violence intervention).”

REPARATIONS ACTIVISTS CALL OUT BLUE STATES FOR USING SLAVERY HISTORY TO FUND BROADER AGENDA

Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson and President Donald Trump have butted heads over law and order in the blue city. (Scott Olson/Getty Images; Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)

The podcast hosts turned to a recent Truth Social post by Trump targeting Illinois leadership over crime.

“Chicago is suffering an unprecedented and particularly violent crime wave that is getting worse by the day,” Trump posted on Oct. 6. “The Federal Government can extinguish it quickly and completely, but the Mayor of Chicago, or the Governor of Illinois, must ask for our help. What is wrong with them? Why aren’t they asking? TIME IS OF THE ESSENCE! President DJT.”

Johnson pushed back against the president’s statement, alleging Trump enriched wealthy Americans while ignoring the demands of “descendants of the formerly enslaved.”

“He’s so sorry. It’s real pathetic, right, because it’s so disingenuous. … This is the president who just released the largest upward transfer of wealth into the hands of the ultrarich at the expense of the demands of those of us who are descendants of the formerly enslaved,” Johnson said.

“The largest upward transfer of wealth at the expense of education, housing, health care, transportation, good-paying jobs, which literally were all the demands of the formerly enslaved.”

TRUMP ADMIN VOWS TO STOP REPARATIONS PROGRAMS, ACCUSES OFFICIALS OF ‘VIRTUE SIGNALING’ TO GET ‘VOTES’

While President Trump didn’t name Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson personally, the Illinois Democrat has been vehemently against reforms imposed by the Trump administration in the Windy City. (Joseph Weiser/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)

Johnson also said Trump “cut [the] violence prevention budget by $800 million,” slamming the president for being concerned “about the wrong borders” as illegal weapons pour into Chicago.

“He cut the ATF budget by 30%. My local police department has worked in tandem with the AFT to get illegal weapons off the streets of Chicago. This year alone, we have removed almost 9,000 illegal weapons off the street.”

The White House dismissed Johnson’s claims and called on the mayor to focus on local public safety.

“Government programs that dole out money based on race are illegal,” a White House spokesperson told Fox News Digital Wednesday. “Chicago would be better served if Mayor Johnson focused more on lowering his city’s homicide rate instead of advocating for divisive, unconstitutional government action.” 

BLACK CHICAGOANS CALL ON REPARATIONS FROM GOVERNMENT, MONEY DEPOSITS LIKE ‘STIMULUS’ CHECKS

According to the mayor’s office, Chicago has seen notable drops in violent crime since Johnson took office in May 2023, including double-digit decreases in homicides, shootings and overall violent crime. 

Chicago has “achieved historic double-digit decreases in crime and violence” in 2025, a spokesperson for Johnson told Fox News Digital, and is on track to see even further decreases in violent crime in 2026, with homicides down 3.8%, shootings down 1.3%and robberies down 20.9% from the same period last year.

While Johnson did not explicitly use the word “reparations” during the interview, a spokesperson pointed Fox News Digital to the city’s reparations initiatives.

Johnson previously signed an executive order establishing a 40-member reparations task force intended to address “historical harms committed against Black Chicagoans and their ancestors.”

In March, Johnson announced the Repair Chicago public engagement initiative aimed at gathering lived experiences from Black residents to inform future municipal policy and direct equity measures.

The push for reparations in the region comes as the federal government ramps up legal scrutiny of local programs. Nearby Evanston, Illinois, launched a first-of-its-kind reparations program in 2021, offering $25,000 grants to eligible Black residents or their direct descendants for housing and home repairs, funded by local taxes on legal recreational marijuana sales.

To date, Evanston has distributed more than $7 million of an allotted $20 million fund. Earlier this year, the city’s Reparations Committee cleared an additional wave of funding for 44 residents.

However, the Trump administration’s Department of Justice (DOJ) has signaled plans to challenge race-conscious distribution models. Assistant Attorney General Harmeet K. Dhillon of the DOJ’s Civil Rights Division previously told Fox News Digital that local officials pushing these measures are “virtue signaling” to win votes.

CHICAGO REPARATIONS ADVOCATES SAY FEDERAL GOV MORALLY OWES ‘7 QUADRILLION DOLLARS’ IN SLAVE LABOR

A White House spokesperson pushed back on Mayor Johnson’s reparations demands in comments to Fox News Digital. (Daniel Boczarski/Getty Images)

Federal intervention is expanding elsewhere as well. In September last year, the DOJ warned officials in Buncombe County, North Carolina, that it would investigate potential civil rights violations if local leaders approved recommendations from the Asheville-Buncombe Community Reparations Commission.

Responding to Johnson’s remarks on the podcast, White House spokeswoman Allison Schuster emphasized that the administration remains committed to dismantling race-based initiatives.

“President Trump was resoundingly elected with a mandate to end divisive, racist policies and restore merit and efficiency,” Schuster told Fox News Digital. 

“DEI ran rampant during the Biden administration, and Americans ultimately paid the price for these destructive policies with a restricted labor pool, higher operational costs and workforce inefficiencies. The Trump administration will always promote equal treatment under the law for every American, regardless of race or ethnicity.”

Joshua Q. Nelson is a reporter for Fox News Digital.

Joshua focuses on cultural trends, education, and public policy. He extensively covered reparations developments across the U.S., the Department of Education, and immigration issues.

Joining Fox News Digital in 2019, he previously graduated from Syracuse University’s Maxwell School of Citizenship and Public Affairs and received the University of Pennsylvania’s Wharton Public Policy Certificate.

Story tips can be sent to joshua.nelson@fox.com and Joshua can be followed on Instagram, Twitter and LinkedIn.
news.summary: A spokesperson urged the mayor to focus on lowering homicide rates instead of advocating race-based government programsThe White House punched back at Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson on Wednesday after the progressive mayor claimed President Donald Trump neglected compensation for descendants of formerly enslaved Black Americans...

news.title: "When You Are Given Gifts, You Take Them": Trump On Accepting Qatar's Air Force One
news.text: President Donald Trump showed off the new Air Force One and defended accepting the luxury jet from the Qatari royal family as he campaigned for Republicans Wednesday in an economically struggling corner of rural Arizona.His first substantive comments after he got off the plane to address the airport rally described learning that the Qataris had "the best of all the 747s." He said he called to ask the country's leader to borrow the aircraft before the emir offered it instead as a gift.Trump accepted the airplane last year despite strong bipartisan criticism, including from some of his staunchest Republican supporters."When you're given gifts, you take 'em, right?" Trump told the crowd in Bullhead City. "When they give you a 747 you say two words: 'thank you.'"Trump was on his second day of a Western campaign swing and was headed to a Republican-leaning US House district in Montana after Arizona, continuing a midterm roadshow designed to rally the GOP. He campaigned in Alaska on Tuesday and in Ohio on Monday.The visits come as the Republican president works to bolster his party in November 3 elections that will determine control of Congress.In Arizona, soaring music played as the former Qatari jet flew low over the local airport where supporters awaited Trump in the heat. The president, wearing his signature red baseball cap, emerged with a wave and a fist bump and slowly descended the stairs as speakers blasted Lee Greenwood's "God Bless the USA," the song that marks Trump's entrance at campaign events.Air Force One, now wearing Trump's new red, white, blue and gold paint scheme, and the Black Mountains filled the background as he started speaking.Mohave County, where Bullhead City is located, has higher poverty and unemployment rates than the state and nation, with a lower per-capita income, according to Census and state unemployment data.Trump also spoke extensively about his aesthetic flourishes around Washington: the White House ballroom that is under construction and a just-completed helipad on the South Lawn, along with a triumphal arch he has planned for the capital city."The fake news media doesn't talk about how well we're doing" as a country, Trump said. Journalists ask him instead about "affordability," he said, pronouncing the word in a dismissive tone.Trump traveled to Arizona to rally support for Republican Andy Biggs, who is seeking to defeat Democratic Governor Katie Hobbs. Republicans running in the state's two competitive US House districts, Jay Feely and Rep. Juan Ciscomani, did not attend the event.Afterward, Trump was heading to Western Montana's 1st District to try to boost Aaron Flint, a former aide to retiring Republican Represntative Ryan Zinke, who was Interior secretary in Trump's first-term Cabinet.Trump has kept up a brisk pace of hour-plus-long rallies - new White House press secretary Katie Zacharia called it a "midterm blitz" - in his effort to stem expected Republican losses and fight a historical trend in which the president's party typically loses seats in elections halfway through their term in the White House.Arizona stands out as the lone swing state among the president's recent stops, though the airport rally was in a county Trump won with 78% of the vote in 2024.His other visits so far in October have taken him into traditionally solid Republican territory - Alabama, Nebraska, Ohio, Tennessee and Texas - as he weathers low approval ratings, rising costs and the Iran war.With under three weeks left in the campaign, the Western swing comes as Trump's party has begun retreating from a handful of battleground U.S. House races and Democrats aim to raise money for candidates who seemed like long shots earlier this year.The shifting money in the final weeks of midterm campaigns reflects an increasingly defensive posture by Republicans, who have already trimmed their expectations in US Senate races, and new aggression from Democrats, who are trying to capitalize on Trump's low public approval.Trump twice won Arizona, in 2016 and 2024, but lost the state in 2020. Montana's 1st District is slightly less Republican overall than the state, which voted for Trump by double digits in each of his three presidential campaigns.Biggs, of Arizona, has been a stalwart ally of the president and assisted Trump's attempt to block certification by the House of Trump's 2020 election defeat. A one-time head of the conservative House Freedom Caucus, he's represented a safe GOP seat since winning election in 2016.He faces Hobbs, who narrowly defeated Republican Kari Lake in the governor's race four years ago. Arizona was long a GOP stronghold, and registered Republicans still outnumber Democrats and independents by a comfortable margin, but voters have repeatedly rejected Trump allies and handed the state's top offices to Democrats.Trump said Biggs "will always stand with law enforcement" and took aim at Hobbs, who he said "does the bidding of the cartels" on the US-Mexico border. Hobbs counters that she has strengthened the border by sending National Guard troops there and has boosted local law enforcement funding.In Montana, Flint won the president's and Zinke's endorsement during the June primary. An Army veteran and talk-radio host, Flint assails progressive Democrats like Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani as part of his campaign.Flint's opponent is Sam Forstag, a Democratic labor union leader and Forest Service smokejumper, a specialized firefighter who gets to fires by aircraft and parachute.(Except for the headline, this story has not been edited by NDTV staff and is published from a syndicated feed.)
news.summary: Trump was on his second day of a Western campaign swing and was headed to a Republican-leaning US House district in Montana after Arizona.
