news.title: Fusionism and its Limits
news.text:
Recent political developments have rekindled longstanding debates over "fusionism," the combination of libertarianism and conservative traditionalism that dominated the American right from roughly the late 1970s through the early years of this century. That dominance has been severely undermined and likely overthrown by the rise of nationalism and "postliberalism." But some would like to revive it. Reason editor Stephanie Slade's important new book Fusionism: Liberty, Virtue, and the Future of the American Right outlines one notable case for such a revival.

I agree with Slade, Jonathan Adler, and others that fusionism is far preferable to nationalism and postliberalism. But I am skeptical about its political viability. In addition, fusionism has significant conceptual flaws. Finally, at least in the short to medium term future, an alliance with "abundance liberals" is probably a more promising political strategy for libertarians than a revival of fusionism.

Despite my relative skepticism about a revival, I readily acknowledge fusionism's significant past achievements, and ongoing superiority over various other tendencies on the conservative right. Between the 1970s and the early 2000s, fusionist conservatives and libertarians (sometimes with the help of moderate/"neoliberal" Democrats) made huge contributions to such achievements as deregulation of many sectors of the economy, reducing tax rates, reinvigorating constitutional protection for property rights and limits on federal government power, and the West's triumph in the Cold War. While early fusionists sometimes undervalued the Civil Rights movement and were soft on racism, over time most of them came to promote color-blindness and and abjuring racial and ethnic discrimination in government policy. They even, for a long time, succeeded in making racial and ethnic color-blindness the dominant approach to such issues in the conservative movement. William F. Buckley and other fusionists also worked to purge the political right of its longstanding tendencies towards anti-Semitism. In combination, these are no small achievements.

The Rise of Right-Wing Nationalism and Postliberalism

But, especially over the last decade, fusionism has been displaced by nationalism as the dominant ideology of the Republican Party and the conservative movement. Where fusionism sought to reconcile traditionalism and liberty, nationalism is a grave menace to liberty across a wide range of issues. Consider Donald Trump's massive tariffs, federal takeovers of numerous private corporations, attempts to use the FCC and other government agencies to undermine free speech, and policy of mass deportations (which threatens the civil liberties and economic future of native-born citizens as well as immigrants).

Instead of color-blindness and nondiscrimination, we now have a conservative movement increasingly permeated with racial and ethnic bigotry and anti-Semitism of the kind fusionists sought to purge. Prominent right-wing "influencers" go so far as to claim we need to bar Indian immigrants because they work too hard and undermine the objectives of "homogeneity" and "maintain[ing] a white majority in the country." Many congressional Republicans also promote religious discrimination in immigration and other policies. In foreign policy, Trump has undermined relations with liberal democratic allies like Canada, Australia, and the nations of the European Union, and kowtowed towards illiberal nationalist authoritarians like Vladimir Putin.

Trump's idiosyncratic personal predilections contribute to some of these developments. But most arise from inherent tendencies of nationalism, which gravitates towards a zero-sum view of the world that leads to expanded government control of the economy, repression of racial and ethnic minorities, undermining civil liberties, and authoritarianism.

The "postliberalism" advocated by many leading right-wing intellectuals and activists is just as bad. Postliberals like Adrian Vermeule and Patrick Deneen are very clear about their desire to massively expand government control over the economy and civil society, and destroy both economic and personal liberties. Unlike nationalism, postliberalism has little mass public support. But it does have considerable influence among the intellectuals and activists who may staff future Republican administrations and congressional offices.

Illiberal big-government nationalism holds a strong sway over the Republican base. The 2024 election dramatically illustrates that. In the 2024 GOP presidential primary, Trump was challenged by Nikki Haley (a prominent advocate of traditional fusionism) and Ron DeSantis (popular governor of a major red state who tried to, in effect, split the difference between MAGA nationalism and pre-2016 conservatism). And, yet, despite the events of January 6, 2021 and numerous other scandals, Trump not only beat these opponents, but did so very easily. While that was partly due to his particular type of charisma, it also highlights the influence of illiberal nationalism over the GOP. Even now, with Trump increasingly unpopular, most congressional Republicans shy away from challenging his worst policies, for fear of losing to MAGA types in GOP primaries. Many of those who are willing to challenge him on major issues have either been ousted in GOP primaries (like Rep. Thomas Massie), or chose not to run for reelection because of the likelihood of suffering that fate (e.g. - Rep. Don Bacon).

Facing a difficult political environment in the 2026 midterm elections, some congressional Republicans have become more willing to criticize a few of Trump's policies, such as the badly mismanaged Iran War. But very few have repudiated his big-government nationalism across the board or called for a return to fusionism.

Perhaps this will all change once Trump leaves the scene. But we shouldn't count on it. At this point, the major likely contenders for the 2028 GOP presidential nomination - Vice-President J.D. Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio - seem like they are vying for the mantle of inheritors of Trump's worst tendencies, not opponents of them.

Inherent Limitations of Fusionism

Even if fusionists do manage to regain control of the Republican Party and the conservative movement, the ideology's inherent limitations might undermine its value. The extent to which fusionism is compatible with strong protections for economic and personal liberty is actually ambiguous. Frank Meyer, a key founder of fusionism in the 1950s and 60s, famously argued that liberty and virtue are mutually reinforcing because liberty is what enables people to be truly virtuous. A person who only does the right thing because he is forced to by the state isn't truly virtuous at all. Think, for example, of a man who only refrains from violence and theft for fear of going to prison. A paragon of virtue he is not.

This position has considerable merit. But most social conservatives, including many otherwise sympathetic to fusionism, don't fully buy it, or even come close. They argue that, at least in many instances, we want to achieve virtuous behavior, regardless of the motivation for it. Or, at least, that doing the right thing for a bad reason is far preferable to not doing it at all. Thus, if you believe that using pornography, prostitution, gambling, taking various drugs, and so on are inherently immoral, then you may well advocate using government power to suppress these activities, even if people who only refrain out of fear of punishment are not as virtuous as those who abjure them voluntarily.

Many conservative fusionists do, in fact, believe that a wide range of consensual activities like the above are inherently evil. Alternatively, many believe that we have to suppress at least some of them out of paternalism. For example, they argue we must suppress drugs, prostitution, and gambling, because people who do these things don't understand what's good for them.

For these reasons, most conservative fusionists have in fact been willing to endorse many policies that severely curtail liberty. Even Ronald Reagan - the president whose administration most exemplified fusionism - promoted a major expansion of the War on Drugs, a federal policy that massively curtails liberty by killing or imprisoning hundreds of thousands people merely because they have used, possessed, or distributed substances the government considers too risky. Reagan's drug policies were not as bad as Trump's policy of outright murdering supposed drug dealers in the Caribbean and Pacific. But they were plenty bad enough, and a notable example of the limitations of fusionism.

Elsewhere, I have argued that, at this moment in political history, the best available potential allies for libertarians are "abundance liberals." They are by no means perfect. But they agree with us - to a large extent - on numerous key issues, including trade, immigration, nuclear power, "YIMBY" housing deregulation, and more. And, like us, they tend to oppose both left and right-wing ethnic identity politics (on which latter point see recent articles by Matt Yglesias and Kelsey Piper). On the whole, they are less paternalistic and less prone to advocate suppression of consensual activities than most fusionist conservatives. They also have considerably greater influence over the Democratic Party and the political left, generally, than fusionists currently have in the Republican Party and the conservative movement.

The left, of course, has its own dangerous illiberal menace in the form of "democratic socialists," whose statism has much in common with that of MAGA nationalists. But this faction is nowhere near dominating the Democratic Party and the political left to the degree that nationalists have come to dominate the right.

None of this proves that libertarians cannot work with fusionist conservatives at all. There are a good many issues on which there is still room for cooperation. I myself have worked with such people in the Society for the Rule of Law, and in the effort to combat Trump's tariffs (where they played crucial roles in the litigation that led to the invalidation of Trump's IEEPA tariff power grab by the Supreme Court and in currently ongoing efforts to challenge his attempts to use other laws to reimpose sweeping tariffs). Some conservative fusionists are more pro-liberty than others. And, for most, there is considerable variation across issues.

And, perhaps, things will be different in a decade or two. The Trumpist moment in right-wing politics may dissipate over time, though it seems unlikely to do so quickly.

Productive cooperation between libertarians and (some) conservatives is still very much possible. But we should recognize that fusionists are unlikely to regain control over the conservative movement anytime soon, and that fusionism has notable inherent limitations. Thus, we should look for other allies, and carefully limit the percentage of our eggs that we put in the fusionist basket. At this point, it cannot safely hold very many of them.
news.summary: Fusionism is far preferable to nationalism and postliberalism. But it has shortcomings of its own, and its political prospects are questionable.
news.author: Ilya Somin,Ryan Curtis

news.title: Katie Zacharia and Natalie Harp’s Intimate Flight With Trump Pictured
news.text:
President Donald Trump’s freshly minted White House press secretary was spotted beaming beside his ever-present aide in a photo from their trip to Alaska.

Katie Zacharia, 41, and Natalie Harp, 35, sat side by side in close proximity to their 80-year-old boss aboard Marine One as they prepared to fly from Elmendorf Air Force Base in Anchorage to Wasilla, Alaska, on Tuesday.

The president’s two blonde subordinates looked eager to speak with him as they huddled inside the aircraft’s cabin, as seen in photos captured by Getty Images photographers Alex Wong and Kent Nishimura.

Trump’s entourage accompanied him on the eight-hour journey to his campaign rally for Alaska Sen. Dan Sullivan on Tuesday.

They were also pictured together on the tarmac at Joint Base Andrews Tuesday beside White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, with Zacharia in a muted blue blazer and Harp in a floral blue dress.

During the Wasilla rally, Trump pardoned Zachary Czuback and Patrick Fleming, co-owners of a vehicle repair shop in Anchorage, who pleaded guilty in 2022 to violating the Clean Air Act.

The two admitted to removing federally mandated emissions-control equipment and tampering with monitoring devices on nearly 40 diesel vehicles between July 2019 and September 2020.

Trump called for Harp to “bring me the pardons!” to which she quickly carried them onstage and handed them to him.

Harp earned the nickname “human printer” for her rapid fulfillment of Trump’s every request, from fetching merchandise, performing Google searches, printing stories from right-wing news sites, and suggesting and typing up his Truth Social posts.

As the president’s special and executive assistant, she earns a taxpayer-funded salary of $150,000 a year.

Zacharia, a former conservative commentator who appeared frequently on Fox and Newsmax, made her White House debut earlier on Tuesday, hosting an awkward 14-minute press briefing that drew criticism from both sides of the aisle.

“I want to thank President Trump for his trust that he has placed in me. I have wanted to work with him for a very long time,” she told reporters. “I’m looking forward to working with each of you as well, especially as we are in the middle of the midterm blitz with energy and excitement never seen before in the history of midterms thanks to President Trump.”

Even some within the White House considered her performance subpar, with one unnamed administration official telling MS NOW’s Jake Traylor that “she needs to get much better, fast. Otherwise, she’ll break [Anthony] Scaramucci’s record.”

Trump, however, was impressed, saying after the briefing, “I thought she was very good.”

news.title: Ohio’s working-class voters rethink support for Trump and the Republican Party
news.text: Warren, Ohio - A decade after U.S. President Donald Trump, a Republican, peeled away working-class and union voters who had long been a cornerstone of Democratic support in Ohio, Democrats and labor leaders see an opening to win back some of them in the Nov. 3 elections.Now midway through his second term, the president’s magic appears to be losing at least some of its luster with blue-collar men and women as rising prices, the Iran war and concerns about his rhetoric prompt some voters to reconsider their support.The state’s reputation as a leading swing state began to fade in 2016 when Trump won strong support from working-class voters who felt their economic concerns were being heard, helping turn Ohio into a reliably Republican state.
news.summary: A shift in Ohio toward Democrats matter in elections that could determine control of the U.S. Congress for Trump's final two years in office.

news.title: The most important US midterm trends I’m seeing
news.text:
‘Voters seem mad that the establishment isn’t elevating their concerns enough.’ Photograph: Saul Loeb/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘Voters seem mad that the establishment isn’t elevating their concerns enough.’ Photograph: Saul Loeb/ReutersThe most important US midterm trends I’m seeingMolly Jong-FastThe one I worry about most is voter anger – which both parties are not taking seriously enough

That chill in the air you are feeling is not the weather, it is the Republicans freaking out about the 2026 midterm elections. Midterms are always referendums on the incumbent, though the party in power usually would rather they weren’t.

This midterm feels less like a referendum on Trumpism than a dirge. It’s easy to see how Republicans got here, lulled into thinking that their guy, Donald Trump, could once again defy political gravity. Trump certainly thought he could.

When it became clear he couldn’t, Trump tried to defy political gravity by federalizing elections and messing with mail-in voting (many would call this cheating) or redrawing the map to gain seats in states like Texas (many would also call this cheating).

Even Trump at his peak couldn’t defy diesel at $6.50 a gallon, and Trump is no longer the deft faux populist he was in his first term. Bored, his eyelids often droop and his mouth often becomes slack during his PM meetings.

Read moreIn a political environment like this where Democrats have about a nine-point advantage, even some of the redder parts of the country seem very much in play. Even some of those redrawn seats in Texas may stay in Democratic hands.

Trump’s mail-in voting plan has been foiled by six and half supreme court justices, the political reality is beginning to sink in and that political reality is looking like a doozy. Turns out doing the exact opposite of what you campaigned on is not that popular. Here are some of stories I have noticed emerging this midterm election cycle.

One of the things I noticed when interviewing political candidates for my podcast Fast Politics was that the cost-of-living crisis looks different in different places. In Maine, a candidate for the second congressional district, Matt Dunlap, told me his voters were worried about heating oil prices. That’s because diesel hit a record national average of $6.51 this week and both diesel and heating oil use a very similar chemical compound.

Maine also starts getting cold in October, so heating oil is a major expense for residents. Bobby Pulido, a Texas congressional candidate and Tejano singer, told me that one of the things that voters in his 15th congressional district are worried about was beef prices, which are about $7 a pound. But Texas cattle ranchers are also not happy about the administration importing beef from South America.

I’ve seen more than a few internet fights about the left v center divide in the Democratic party but there are candidates who represent both the left and the center. These are candidates who have been endorsed by the Blue dogs and Bernie Sanders.

They are populist moderates running in purple(ish) districts. I’ve talked to a lot of Democratic candidates who describe a political atmosphere which fueled by voter rage is not left v right as much as down v up.

These candidates include Pennsylvania’s Bob Brooks, Wisconsin’s Rebecca Cooke, Montana’s Sam Forstag and Ohio’s Brian Poindexter. All these candidates are either very involved in their unions or, in the case of Cooke, in a union family. They are centrists and populists, something that at least theoretically shouldn’t coexist.

Iowa has two major elections this cycle – in both the Democratic candidates are polling ahead, and in both the Democrats are running in an “up v down” framing. But the reason that Iowa, a state Trump won by 13.2 points in 2024 and 9.4 points in 2016, is so deeply in play this cycle may have more to do with environmental contamination than inflationary pressures. Iowa is in the middle of a cancer crisis; it has the second highest rate of cancer in the US. For people over the age of 50, it’s 10% higher than the national average.

Thomas Frank wrote about how Republicans in Kansas used culture war issues to get working-class people to vote for Republicans, who then enacted pro-oligarch legislation. Well, weirdly, Kansas has emerged as a focal point this cycle.

The Wall Street Journal reported Roger Marshall, a Republican senator, was met with boos, hisses and jeering at the Kansas state fair Senate debate. He is running against Adam Hamilton, a popular Democrat and mega-church pastor. Recent reporting details Marshall’s predatory behavior regarding debt collections for his gynecological practice. The Cook Political Report recently shifted the race from likely Republican to lean Republican, which for a state Trump won by more than 16 points is kind of striking.

In less than two years Republicans have gone from shocking bravado to desperately begging for votes. Vance went on the rightwing tech-bro podcast all in to ask voters to “give us another chance, or give us another couple of years, to continue to work on the amazing things that we’ve been doing for the past two years”.

In Iowa at a rally for Republicans where Senate candidate Ashley Hinson didn’t show up, Vance pleaded with the crowd. “Whenever you hear me talk during this midterm campaign, I’ll say Rome was not built in a day because we know there’s a lot of work to do.”

And on X, Matt Gaetz, a former Republican congressman, posted: “Bro we need your vote. I hate the war too. But the Democrats want to trans your kids.” It was such a clear distillation of the Republican closing message of these midterms: we didn’t do any of the stuff you elected us to do but Democrats want to … and then you can insert any of the culture warrior tropes that the party has bantered about.

There are other trends, I’m seeing. The one that I worry the most about is voter anger. In 2018, we saw a rejection of Trumpism but voters didn’t seem as furious. It feels like both parties aren’t taking voter anger seriously enough.

Sure, voters want to kick out Republicans, we can see this in the polls, but voters seem mad that the establishment isn’t elevating their concerns enough. Datacenters and government corruption are issues that 80% of voters support action on. If the establishment fails to address these issues with authenticity and zeal, both parties are going to have real problems.

Molly Jong-Fast is the host of the Fast Politics pod, contributing writer for the times and an analyst for MS Now

news.title: WSJ Editorial Board to Trump: get a grip on inflation — or else
news.text:
President Donald Trump has repeatedly referred to the American economy under his second term as a "golden age." A conservative editorial board disagrees strongly with that self-assessment.

"The Labor Department’s inflation report on Wednesday was disappointing, and it explains why voters remain unhappy about the economy," wrote The Wall Street Journal's editorial board on Wednesday. "Prices are rising faster than wages."

The newspaper continued, "The consumer-price index rose 0.6 percent in September and is up 3.7 percent over 12 months. Energy accounted for more than half of the increase as supply disruptions from the Iran war push up prices. Consumers will get some relief when oil and fuel supplies return to normal, but it could be awhile."

From there, the editorial board briefly surveyed the landscape in prices, explaining why energy, food and other prices are rising in a landscape of erratic tariffs and a prolonged war in the Middle East.

"The lesson for monetary policy is that the Federal Reserve under former Chairman Jerome Powell was premature in easing in late 2024 and last year. Inflation rebounded each time," the editorial board wrote. "Mr. Powell, who remains a Fed Governor, did no favors for successor Kevin Warsh."

Warsh's biggest obstacle at present, though, may be Trump himself.

"President Trump wants the Fed to cut rates as he always does, rain or shine, spring, summer, winter or fall," the editorial board concluded. "But the Fed clearly has more work to do against inflation. Mr. Trump ought to give Mr. Warsh the support to squash it. That is, unless the President wants inflation to remain a losing issue for Republicans in 2028 the way it looks like it will be for the party on Election Day this year."

Conservatives are not alone in urging Warsh to stand firm against Trump's pressure. Dr. Robert J. Shapiro, an economic who served as a top adviser for President Bill Clinton, told AlterNet in August that "Trump has been attacking the Fed for as long as he's been in office for not cutting interest rates. But you don't cut interest rates when inflation is rising, because cutting rates stimulates the economy — meaning you increase demand without increasing supply, so prices go up. Powell refused to cut rates because he said, in effect, 'We're in an inflationary period; once we contain inflation, we can cut rates.' Trump has made that much harder by increasing inflation through both the tariffs and the effects of the war on Iran."

He continued, "Even [Kevin] Warsh, Trump's handpicked successor to [Jerome] Powell, hasn't cut rates. But the market believes there's a significant possibility that he will, given the pressure Trump has been putting on him — and in anticipation of that, they've been driving long-term rates up. We'll see what Warsh does. My own guess is that he'll wait until right before or right after the election to raise rates, because he doesn't set policy alone — interest rate policy is made by a committee at the Federal Reserve comprising the seven members of the Board plus five of the regional bank presidents, and there's increasing pressure among them to raise rates."

news.title: Trump voters scold president to start ‘taking care of the people in your country’: NYT
news.text:
Some voters who sent President Donald Trump back to the White House have a pointed message for him ahead of the midterms.

Grocery shoppers who backed Trump in 2024 told The New York Times for a Wednesday report that rising prices have left several of them frustrated, with a retired nurse in Maine telling the president, "you should be taking care of the people in your country."

Rebecca Guerrette, an independent, said she was unhappy with the economy and called the war with Iran a "waste of money." "I think Trump did a better job as president like eight years ago," Guerrette told The Times. She said living costs have climbed in recent years while paychecks have not kept pace, adding that she probably would not cast a ballot in the Senate race between Sen. Susan Collins (R-ME) and Democrat Troy Jackson.

The Times interviewed shoppers in Iowa, Ohio, Maine and Michigan, all home to closely watched Senate races, as consumer prices run 3.7 percent higher than a year ago, according to Bureau of Labor Statistics figures released Wednesday. Food costs are up 2.5 percent over the same period, with The Times pointing to the Iran war's toll on fuel and shipping costs. The outlet reported that a growing number of Republican candidates are distancing themselves from Trump amid the squeeze. 

Trump campaigned on making America more affordable and later told NBC News, "I won on groceries."

Angel Hartmier of Ohio said 2024 was the first election she had ever voted in, and she had hoped Trump would bring prices down. "It was bad before, but now it's way worse," said Hartmier, a single mother of three. "I am very disappointed, I thought things would change." She said she was unsure about the midterms. "I might vote again, because I want things to get better," she said. "But I did it for the first time and it all went sideways."

Jessy Hakizimana, who owns an excavating company in Iowa, said he now hunts for coupons, something he never used to do. "I don't think he has lowered prices for anything," he said. Of his 2024 vote, he said, "It's too soon to say I regret it. But so far, it doesn't look good."

Not every voter has turned. Carolyn Calcutt, a retired teacher in Michigan, said Trump was doing an "amazing" job on the economy, while Dan Ratliff from Ohio described it as "humming along."

White House spokesman Matthew Middleton defended the Trump administration's economic record, saying the president had a strong pro-growth agenda.

news.title: The S&P 500 Has Risen 30.6% in the First 20 Months of Trump's Second Term, Just Ahead of the 28.5% Gain Over the Same Stretch of His First Term. Here's Why That Comparison Matters for Investors Heading Into the Midterms.
news.text:
Barring a fourth-quarter collapse of epic proportions, the S&P 500 (^GSPC -1.11%) will notch another positive annual performance in 2026, meaning that of the six years President Donald Trump has been commander in chief, 2018 still ranks as the worst year for stocks.

During that year, the S&P 500 lost 5.2% due largely to a trade war with China, one that some experts believe Trump sought out. Fast-forward to September 2026, and over 20 months of Trump's second term, stocks are performing remarkably similarly to what was seen during Trump's first term.

Actually, the S&P 500 (as of Sept. 30) is actually pacing ahead of where it was in Trump's first term, increasing 30.6% since Trump took office the second time, versus 28.5% in the first 20 months of his first term. Let's get into why that comparison matters.

History matters

Good investors are often students of market history because past scenarios have a way of repeating, as do investors' responses to those situations. That's pertinent to discussing the performance of the S&P 500 during the first 20 months of the two Trump terms because midterm election years are historically the worst for stocks. The S&P 500's average gain in a midterm election year is just 4.9%, less than half the market's historical average gain.

But the market is bucking that trend this year. Historically, the best year for the market is the third year of the presidential cycle, which suggests 2027 could be another solid year for the market.

There's another factor at play. In 2018, Democrats gained control of Congress, and due to macroeconomic headwinds such as high inflation and broader affordability concerns, political pundits are implying it's almost a foregone conclusion that Democrats will gain control of the House in this fall's election, and also have a credible shot at earning a Senate majority. 

Regardless of the preferred party, investors may breathe a sigh of relief because history confirms that a divided government is usually beneficial to stocks. It acts as a "handcuff" on either party, preventing it from enacting sweeping legislation that could roil financial markets. For those keeping score at home, the Vanguard S&P 500 surged 28.9% in 2019 under Trump and a Democratic congressional majority.

How to invest

Of course, investors can't directly buy the S&P 500. But they can buy an exchange-traded fund that tracks the index, and the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (VOO -1.09%) is an ideal option thanks to its direct correlation with the index and a low expense ratio of 0.03%, or $3 annually for $10,000 invested.

Admittedly, comparing the S&P 500's performances in the first 20 months of Trump's first and second terms has some bumps. Even when accounting for the trade war with China, the 2018 environment was far more sanguine than it is today.

That's certainly true from a geopolitical perspective. The war in Iran pushed oil prices (and inflation) to uncomfortably high levels. Not to be lost in that shuffle is the fact that the war in Ukraine has now lasted longer than U.S. involvement in World War II.

The point is, stocks have been resilient in the face of a variety of challenges. Whether any politician deserves credit for that is a conversation for another day, but ahead of Election Day and the start of 2027, that sturdiness is an encouraging sign.
news.summary: It hasn't always been easy, but the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF is pacing ahead of where it was during the first 20 months of President Trump's first term in office.

news.title: Trump, 80, Turns Pope’s Cancer Into Rant About Himself
news.text:
President Donald Trump has turned a question about Pope Leo’s cancer diagnosis into a rant about himself.

Trump, 80, briefly spoke to the media at Bullhead International Airport on Wednesday, after attending a rally in Bullhead City, Arizona.

The president was asked about Pope Leo XIV’s health, following the Vatican revealing on Tuesday that the pontiff, 71, had undergone surgery to remove the lower lobe of his right lung, after being diagnosed with lung cancer.

Tests identified pulmonary adenocarcinoma, a common type of lung cancer. Doctors did not disclose the cancer’s stage or how far it had progressed. The pope has canceled all of his audiences until October 20 as he recovers.

“The surgery was completed successfully, within the expected timeframe and as planned, and the Holy Father has returned to his room,” the Vatican posted on Tuesday.

Trump told reporters on Wednesday, “I want to see Pope Leo get well.”

He added, “I hear the prognosis for that type of a problem... it’s a cancer, it’s big stuff anytime you have cancer, but the prognosis seems to be good. I’ve watched... and we just want to wish him our love and our best wishes.”

The president then immediately began discussing Pope Leo’s eldest brother, Louis Prevost, who has shared his support of Trump and the MAGA movement on Facebook, even meeting the president at the White House days after Leo was declared pope.

“His brother’s a friend of mine who’s a great... he’s a fantastic guy and his wife,” Trump said.

“You know, they’re big Trump supporters,” the senior president bragged. “They have MAGA all over their house. And I can say that his brother loves him a lot, loves the pope a lot and that’s good. That’s good enough for me. But I just want to wish him well. Get better fast.”

The Daily Beast has reached out to the White House for comment.

The pope has previously condemned Trump’s war with Iran, as well as ICE raids and immigration crackdowns, which he labeled “extremely disrespectful.”

By comparison, Prevost’s extreme social media posts have not only praised Trump, but attacked the trans community and Democrats. He also once shared a video that referred to former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi as a “c---.”

Trump invited Prevost to the White House in May last year, telling reporters ahead of the meeting, “Did you know that he lives in Florida? He’s got MAGA, he’s got Trump, and I look forward to getting him to the White House. I want to shake his hand. I want to give him a big hug.”

The president previously expressed his preference for the pope’s brother and slammed the pontiff in a wild Truth Social post in April.

“Pope Leo is WEAK on Crime, and terrible for Foreign Policy,” Trump wrote, adding, “I like his brother Louis much better than I like him, because Louis is all MAGA. He gets it, and Leo doesn’t! I don’t want a Pope who thinks it’s OK for Iran to have a Nuclear Weapon.”

The post also claimed, “If I wasn’t in the White House, Leo wouldn’t be in the Vatican.”

Prevost was invited to Trump’s tacky 80th birthday MMA fight at the White House in June, and was pictured mingling with Vice President JD Vance.

Prevost also sat next to Vance during Leo’s inauguration at the Vatican in May last year.
